item.content:encoded:
The wildest weekend of the college football season was nonstop drama from the noon slate all the way through to the final snap of the night out West, so naturally that had a massive impact on the way the postseason looks. As much focus as there is on the expansion to the College Football Playoff, this year there are still only 12 teams and the at-large spots are getting tight given the number of potential 10–2/9–3 teams in the Big 12, Big Ten and SEC.
That’s reflected in the Sports Illustrated latest bowl projections going into Week 8, which sees some fascinating CFP matchups from the first round (Texas Tech’s Joey McGuire gets his much-anticipated game against Notre Dame) all the way through to a rematch of last year’s title game in Las Vegas. The rest of the postseason is full of equally fun games, from the possibility of Bill Belichick getting drenched in mayo against Penn State, another West Coast meeting between USC and Texas (in Vegas), an old Big Eight reunion in the Liberty Bowl and a heck of a FBS caper for North Dakota State against a fellow Group of 6 power in the desert.

item.content:encoded:
カブス・鈴木誠也外野手（３２）の市場価値が高騰中だ。今季限りで５年契約が満了となり、来季の所属球団がどこになるのか米メディアを連日にぎわせている。
今季は１４３試合に出場して打率２割７分、２６本塁打、８６打点、ＯＰＳ０・８４１をマークし、守備力の向上も評価されて右翼手部門でゴールドグラブ賞の最終候補にも残った。攻守にわたる安定した活躍で外野手としてＦＡ市場の目玉の一人となっている。
当然、カブスとしては来季も必要な戦力。球団の専門メディア「ＣＵＢＢＩＥＳ ＣＲＩＢ」は１７日（日本時間１８日）に「イアン・ハップと鈴木という主力野手の退団に直面している。１人は新たな契約で呼び戻す方法を探す必要がある」と流出阻止を唱えた。
鈴木の契約は５年総額８５００万ドル（約１３５億円＝当時）で年平均１７００万ドル（約２７億円）だった。同メディアはプロスポーツ選手の契約などをデータ化する米サイト「ｓｐｏｔｒａｃ」がはじき出した「４年総額９０００万ドル（約１４２億円）」「平均年俸２２５０万ドル（約５６億２０００万円）」の予想価格をもとに「カブスは鈴木を呼び戻すためにあらゆる手を尽くすべきだ」と資金の捻出を迫った。
ところが、同日のうちに「ｓｐｏｔｒａｃ」が示した鈴木の〝適正価格〟は「４年総額１億０９９６万ドル（約１７３億８０００万円）」まで上昇。一気に２０００万ドル（約３２億円）近くも跳ね上がった格好だ。
鈴木にとっては選手としてそれだけ高い評価を得ている証しでもあるが、価格が高騰するほど残留の可能性が低くなっていくことも考えられる。波乱含みのオフとなりそうだ。

item.title: [Sportsnet.ca] Rays’ Aranda leaning on advice from Blue Jays’ Kirk during post-season
item.dc:creator: Shi Davidi
item.description: CLEVELAND – Jonathan Aranda and Alejandro Kirk are childhood friends, and before the post-season started, the Tampa Bay Rays first baseman reached out to the Toronto Blue Jays catcher for some advice. “I was like, ‘Hey, do you have any tips for me moving forward here in October?’ And his main suggestion was, just have fun, just have fun and be yourself,” Aranda said through interpreter Kevin Vera ahead of ALCS Game 5. “That's honestly helped me a lot to kind of slow the game down and enjoy the m
item.content:encoded:
CLEVELAND – Jonathan Aranda and Alejandro Kirk are childhood friends, and before the post-season started, the Tampa Bay Rays first baseman reached out to the Toronto Blue Jays catcher for some advice.
“I was like, ‘Hey, do you have any tips for me moving forward here in October?’ And his main suggestion was, just have fun, just have fun and be yourself,” Aranda said through interpreter Kevin Vera ahead of ALCS Game 5. “That's honestly helped me a lot to kind of slow the game down and enjoy the moment and embrace this challenge of what is October baseball.”
Aranda went 0-for-10 through the first three games of the best-of-seven against the Cleveland Guardians before breaking out with three hits, a walk, two RBIs and two runs scored in Saturday's 7-3 win in Game 4.
He and Kirk “talk every day, we're best friends, we're brothers,” and added that “he’s someone that I have by my side.”
Last year, they both went to the all-star game together, but Aranda’s season was truncated by a fractured left wrist suffered July 31, a factor in the Rays falling out of playoff contention.
Still, when the Blue Jays advanced to the World Series, Aranda flew in to follow Kirk, saying “it was a big thing for me to go see him, for us, to see each other in the World Series.”
“In that moment last year, I kind of visualized myself in the same scenario,” he continued. “So now, fast-forward a year later, I use it as motivation right now. Hopefully I can make those dreams that I had last year a reality and help this team to a World Series berth.”

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees have several paths they could take in free agency this offseason.
If history repeats itself, they will be quite successful.
One of the top names floating is that of Tarik Skubal of the Los Angeles Dodgers. Do the Yankees stand a chance?
Yankees Prediction Points To Skubal Opportunity
Christopher Kline of FanSided unveiled his latest rankings of Skubal's potential landing spots.
Of the eight teams he mentioned, New York comes in at No. 4.
This isn't a bad spot to be for an organization that generally thrives on its perfectly imperfect starting rotation.
But that certainly doesn't mean they're the most likely ballclub to acquire to veteran southpaw.
"It would require Hal Steinbrenner and the front office to basically sign off on a blank check, but the Yankees' ALDS loss to the Rays was a sobering defeat," Kline explained. "There are cracks in the foundation. Many of those cracks are injury-related and concentrated in the lineup; Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodón is as strong a four-man gauntlet as any rotation in MLB. The Yankees also have Ryan Weathers, Will Warren and top prospects like Elmer Rodríguez and Carlos Lagrange for depth.
"Still, the Yankees know the importance of depth, especially as their non-Schlittler core ages and becomes more injury-prone. Skubal provides stability and instantly lends credibility to any postseason aspirations. Schlittler-Skubal becomes the most fearsome pitching duo in baseball. Never say never."
Sobering is perhaps the best way to describe how their campaign ended.
Taking it a step further, the value of depth became all the more clear for the Yankees after their star slugger Aaron Judge was sidelined for much of the season.
This forced New York to rely on their younger stars who tend to play in the shadows.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post New York Yankees Prediction Reveals Likelihood of Tarik Skubal Acquisition appeared first on HEAVY.

item.title: [fansided.com] Ranking Tarik Skubal suitors from favorites to dark horses
item.dc:creator: Christopher Kline
item.description: Tarik Skubal and the Los Angeles Dodgers were swept out of the NLCS by the 103-win Milwaukee Brewers, a refreshing change of pace after two years of Dodgers dominance — and a helpful reminder to the MLB owners that payroll alone does not determine winning. item.content:encoded:
Tarik Skubal and the Los Angeles Dodgers were swept out of the NLCS by the 103-win Milwaukee Brewers, a refreshing change of pace after two years of Dodgers dominance — and a helpful reminder to the MLB owners that payroll alone does not determine winning. It also leaves Skubal with a more difficult decision in free agency than many expected.
The Dodgers will not re-sign Skubal before the lockout in December, as there's simply too much risk without knowing how the salary cap will function come 2027. Really regardless of how MLB's labor dispute plays out, however, Los Angeles will hope to retain Skubal, who is still rightly regarded as the most bankable ace in baseball. The question is: Are the Dodgers the favorites for his services? Let's rank all realistic suitors, from least to most realistic.
8. Philadelphia Phillies
The Phillies are desperate and the Phillies typically spend money. Not necessarily as liberally as fans would like, but it's not impossible to imagine Dave Dombrowski — with the World Series window closing rapidly on this aging core — deciding that Skubal is worth an all-in push.
It would give Philadelphia the most talented rotation in MLB between Skubal, Zack Wheeler, Cristopher Sánchez, Jesús Luzardo and Aaron Nola, four of whom could compete for NL Cy Young next season. There's also Andrew Painter, a former top prospect who came into his own down the stretch and delivered big outs in the postseason, to provide depth.
The Phillies probably have enough money wrapped up in that rotation (and in Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber and Trea Turner) to be turned off of paying Skubal top dollar, but it's a fun thought for a team hoping to lean even more on run prevention moving forward.
7. Boston Red Sox
The Red Sox wielded one of the deepest and most reliable rotations in MLB last season; that was with top ace Garrett Crochet on the IL. Upon Crochet's return, Boston will have a compelling blend of experience (Crochet, Ranger Suárez) and emerging youth (Payton Tolle, Jake Bennett) to throw at their opponents.
Then again, they know the toll injuries can take, and Sonny Gray — probably their best regular season starter this past season — is now a free agent. The Red Sox could simply line up a new contract for Gray and be content, but why not aim higher? Skubal has proven remarkably durable over the years and he offers Boston a much longer window as Crochet's partner in crime. Suddenly, the Red Sox have the best one-two punch in baseball and it wouldn't be especially close.
After the Yankees lit them up in the Wild Card round (and after Boston's top arms couldn't pitch deep into either postseason game), there's pressure for a big swing.
6. Chicago Cubs
There's no doubting the Cubs' ability to generate offense, but the rotation has been a sore spot for years now. Jed Hoyer has shown a great appetite for spending in free agency of late; the Alex Bregman signing was a real flex. That said, Chicago needs to allocate more resources toward pitching. The Edward Cabrera trade went belly up. Shōta Imanaga is a free agent now, as are trade deadline pickups Kevin Gausman and Clay Holmes.
Chicago will get help internally with both Cade Horton and Justin Steele returning from season-long elbow injuries; Ben Brown, who finally broke out in 2026, should also be back in the mix. Beyond them, however, it's pretty grim. Matthew Boyd and Javier Assad can eat innings in the regular season, but neither has proven able to pitch deep in October — at least not consistently.
Skubal would deliver Chicago the frontline ace it has long lacked, with a solid scaffolding of talent behind him. The Cubs would be much better positioned to challenge Milwaukee in the division and potentially emerge from a crowded National League field.
5. Detroit Tigers
Skubal has made it clear he would've spent his entire career in Detroit if it was up to him. All the Tigers need to do is come through with a competitive offer. While last year's surprise Framber Valdez signing was a positive indication of the front office's competitive intent, there's a reason no Skubal extension ever came to fruition — or even remotely close.
A client of Scott Boras, Skubal was never inclined to sign an extension. But the Tigers' offers weren't even in the parking lot, much less the ballpark. Detroit will need to scale up its ambition significantly if it wants to lure Skubal back to the midwest.
All that said, Skubal has an affection for Detroit that's worth mentioning. The Tigers also desperately need a frontline ace in Skubal's mold. Young bucks like Troy Melton, Keider Montero, Jackson Jobe and River Ryan are very talented, but the Tigers don't really have an established vet besides Valdez, who was a mess last season.
4. New York Yankees
The Yankees tend to flex their muscles in free agency, although with diminishing returns in recent years. New York is no longer the most lucrative destination for a lot of A-tier stars. Juan Soto a couple years ago, Kyle Tucker last winter; the Yankees are getting outbid pretty consistently these days. That has not stopped New York from stockpiling stars, though, especially in the rotation.
It would require Hal Steinbrenner and the front office to basically sign off on a blank check, but the Yankees' ALDS loss to the Rays was a sobering defeat. There are cracks in the foundation. Many of those cracks are injury-related and concentrated in the lineup; Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodón is as strong a four-man gauntlet as any rotation in MLB. The Yankees also have Ryan Weathers, Will Warren and top prospects like Elmer Rodríguez and Carlos Lagrange for depth.
Still, the Yankees know the importance of depth, especially as their non-Schlittler core ages and becomes more injury-prone. Skubal provides stability and instantly lends credibility to any postseason aspirations. Schlittler-Skubal becomes the most fearsome pitching duo in baseball. Never say never.
3. Toronto Blue Jays
The Blue Jays have steadily become the most aggressive front office in the American League. After finishing runner-up in the Juan Soto and Shohei Ohtani sweepstakes, Toronto extended Vladimir Guerrero Jr. at a $500 million price point and signed Dylan Cease in the early days of free agency last winter. A disappointing season should not preclude Toronto from maintaining its all-in approach; if anything, it's more motivation for the Blue Jays to stack talent. This team was in the World Series a year ago.
Toronto is a great market, with a vibrant local culture and an entire country behind the Blue Jays. That ought to appeal to the vanity of a star like Skubal, who would team up with the projected AL Cy Young runner-up in Cease. The Jays also made a savvy trade for José Soriano at the deadline, adding another premium arm in his prime. Trey Yesavage, once healthy, could resume his ascent to stardom. The talent is there.
Skubal solidifies Toronto as a legitimate World Series contender coming into 2027. Moreover, the Jays have a lot of money coming off the books, which should free up the front office to spend recklessly where it counts. Toronto is always the "dark horse" in these top-dollar bidding wars, but ruling out the Blue Jays would be foolish.
2. Los Angeles Dodgers
It's impossible to rule out the incumbents. Los Angeles made the Skubal trade in part because of their deep farm system — and in part because it set the stage for a potential long-term partnership. There's a reason small-market front offices were unwilling to match L.A.'s outgoing package (see: Brewers). The Dodgers could afford to trade two of the 50ish best prospects in baseball because the team can feel reasonably good about both competing for a World Series this season (oh well) and re-signing Skubal when he hits the open market.
An NLCS loss does complicate the situation somewhat, not to mention the unknowability of upcoming labor disputes. The Dodgers' loss was a direct result of investing hundreds of millions of dollars in stars who are beginning to decline. Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman, Shohei Ohtani, Will Smith, Tyler Glasnow and Blake Snell are all on the wrong side of 30; Tucker will join that list next season. Los Angeles will endure more and more diminishing returns.
That said, nothing (besides a strict salary cap) can really stop the Dodgers from compensating for declining stars by signing more expensive stars, even if it leaves the cap sheet in utter chaos five years from now. That has been L.A.'s strategy to date; it was part of the logic behind the Skubal trade. The Dodgers still arguably represent Skubal's best chance to win a World Series, which will no doubt be part of the calculus if another team can't dramatically outspend them.
1. New York Mets
If any team can blow L.A.'s offer out of the water, it's the Mets. Steve Cohen is baseball's richest owner and New York has consistently tossed its hat in the ring for MLB's premium free agents. Juan Soto's $765 million contract set a new record; Skubal very well could set a record for pitchers.
The Mets are coming off of a last-place season, too, which only fuels anxiety in the fan base. It should also fuel aggression in the front office. David Stearns is under pressure to prove that he has what it takes to win in New York. Skubal would join an emerging ace in Nolan McLean, plus other whippersnappers like Zac Thornton and Jonah Tong. The Mets need depth besides, as Kodai Senga and Sean Manaea look more like bullpen arms these days. New York, however, is the one non-Dodgers team with enough money to sign Skubal and pursue other targets.
If the Dodgers get spooked by the shadow of their own payroll, which is more likely than ever, the Mets are the logical team we can expect to swoop in and win the Skubal bidding war outright.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Back-and-Forth ALCS Could Spell Trouble for Brewers in World Series
item.dc:creator: Curt Bishop
item.description: The Milwaukee Brewers made quick work of the Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League Championship Series to secure their first trip to the World Series in 44 years. Now, the Brewers are awaiting the winner of the American League Championship Series between the Cleveland Guardians and Tampa Bay Rays, which is tied at two games apiece heading into Sunday's Game 5. The series will go at least six games at this point, which means whoever wins it will only have a few days off before the series beg
item.content:encoded:
The Milwaukee Brewers made quick work of the Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League Championship Series to secure their first trip to the World Series in 44 years. Now, the Brewers are awaiting the winner of the American League Championship Series between the Cleveland Guardians and Tampa Bay Rays, which is tied at two games apiece heading into Sunday's Game 5.
The series will go at least six games at this point, which means whoever wins it will only have a few days off before the series begins. This could ultimately spell some trouble for the Brewers, who have a ton of extra rest.
How extra rest can affect teams
Extra rest can help. The Washington Nationals had a week over before the 2019 World Series while the Houston Astros only had two days. Washington proceeded to win the first two games on the road and ultimately win the series in seven games.
However, there have been plenty of cases in which extra rest hasn't exactly been kind to teams. The Detroit Tigers had a week off before the 2006 World Series, while the St. Louis Cardinals won the NLCS in seven games and only had one day. St. Louis made quick work of the Tigers, winning in five games.
The same thing happened to Detroit in 2012 when they swept the ALCS and waited around for the San Francisco Giants to come back from 3-1 to win the series. At that point, the Giants had the momentum and ultimately swept the Tigers.
The 2007 Colorado Rockies and 2015 New York Mets also had extra rest before the World Series and were eliminated quickly. So, it can certainly hurt at times.
Perhaps it could ultimately help the Brewers instead. There's really no way of knowing for sure, as it can work both ways. But things will get interesting if the ALCS goes the full seven games. The winner of that series would only have two days off before the series while Milwaukee will have had over a week.
A case could be made that it just gives the Brewers more time to prepare, and that is certainly true. But teams can also lose their edge when they aren't playing for a week or more before the World Series, so it will be very interesting to see just how it affects the Brewers as they prepare for their first World Series since 1982.
Curt Bishop is a freelance sports writer who graduated from Maryville University of St. Louis with a Bachelor of Arts degree in the field of Communication and currently writes as a contributor for various platforms covering Major League Baseball. Curt’s work includes covering trade and free agency predictions, as well as rumors and news. item.content:encoded:
Will the Phillies trade Bryce Harper this offseason? It’s very unlikely. Harper, one of only two well above average hitters for the Phillies in 2026, has a full no-trade clause. He goes only if he wants to go. Harper had repeatedly said that
But if the Phillies are seeking real change this offseason, every potential move has to be on the table.
Should the Phillies keep Harper heading into year nine of his 13-year contract or should Dave Dombrowski make a seismic trade and move on from “The Showman?”
Here’s part two of Phillies Nation’s Stay or Go series. Vote in our poll below the article.
Past editions:
Destiny Lugardo — Site Director: Stay
Flipping Harper for multiple lineup pieces would represent dramatic change, but Harper has a full-no trade clause and is committed to Philly for the next five years. If he leaves, it’s because he wants to go elsewhere. I’m not a mind reader, but I don’t think Harper is quite there yet. It could happen eventually, but not now.
Ty Daubert — Editorial Director: Stay
According to OPS+, the Phillies had two regulars who produced at an above-average offensive clip in 2026: Kyle Schwarber (128) and Harper (131). Philadelphia needs more capable, effective hitters, and Harper was its best this season. The team could probably use some shaking up after another early exit, but moving on from Harper would only make the underwhelming lineup harder to bulk up. If anything, his productive 162-game, 107-walk year should give the Phillies a bit of additional confidence in his abilities as he heads into his age-34 season.
Bailey Digh — Staff Writer: Stay
The Phillies are going to try to win in 2027. Harper will help with that. He remains one of baseball’s best hitters. He was one of the few things that did not go wrong for the Phillies this year. There’s so much to do this offseason for this club, and there’s going to be a lockout. This offseason isn’t one to make a major move like trading Harper, an idea that only gets thrown out there from people who don’t work for the Phillies.
Nathan Ackerman — Staff Writer: Stay
The Phillies this offseason are going to need to make changes, while resisting the idea of making changes for the sake of making changes if they can’t execute the right changes. Any attempt to move Harper would qualify as that. A team whose offense is arguably its weakest unit – that’s saying something, given the bullpen, which should be much easier to remake – should not try to jettison the player who posted their highest regular-season OPS while playing in all 162 games, before producing in the short postseason. And as bad as the on-field impact would be, the organizational optics would perhaps be just as bad.

item.content:encoded:
Game 5 of the ALCS between the Tampa Bay Rays and Cleveland Guardians takes place on Sunday afternoon, and these teams are knotted at two games apiece after Tampa Bay won Game 4.
There are a ton of props to consider in Game 5 of the ALCS, including a home run prop or two as these teams look to deliver a key blow before the series shifts back to Tampa Bay on Monday.
Drew Rasmussen (14 home runs allowed in the regular season, two in the postseason) and Parker Messick (17 home runs allowed in the regular season, one in the postseason) are on the mound in this game.
The total (6.5) is pretty low in this matchup, so we may not see a ton of offense.
While betting on home runs is a fun way to get involved in the action, these props are extremely tough to hit with the pitching in the postseason. Still, there have been a few long balls in this series, and I’m targeting one player that has already gone deep over the course of the first four games to stay hot on Sunday.
Best MLB Home Run Prop Bet Picks for ALCS Game 5
Chase DeLauter to Hit a Home Run (+970)
Chase DeLauter homered 16 times during the regular season, and he took Drew Rasmussen deep in Game 1.
The Guardians youngster was 1-for-3 against the Rays ace in the series opener, and he’s 2-for-4 against him in the regular season in his career.
DeLauter is dangerous against right-handed pitching, homering 13 times while posting an .808 OPS during the regular season.
He’s also been hot in this series, picking up five hits, three RBIs and three runs scored in four games. Overall, he’s hitting .294 with two doubles in a homer in the 2026 postseason.
There are worse bets to make at nearly 10/1 odds in Game 5.
Junior Caminero to Hit a Home Run (+497)
During the regular season, Junior Caminero hit 42 home runs and was elite against left-handed pitching.
He had a .287 batting average, a .916 OPS and homered eight times against southpaws. He has not had a ton of success against Messick in his career (1-for-12), but the lefty did allow 17 home runs in the 2026 regular season.
At some point, Caminero is going to get a hold of a ball, as he’s yet to go deep in the playoffs. Still, Caminero is hitting, picking up at least one hit in three games in this series, including two doubles.
This prop has skyrocketed all the way to +497 with Messick on the mound, but the Guardians’ bullpen has been taxed over the last few days and could be vulnerable to a long ball.
With just one game to bet on, I’m going to take a shot on the best power hitter for either team to leave the yard on Sunday.
Odds refresh periodically and are subject to change.

item.title: [FanSided] Projecting MLB free agency deals for Tarik Skubal and baseball's biggest stars
item.dc:creator: Christopher Kline
item.description: MLB free agency takes on a new urgency this winter with a Dec. 1 lockout on the horizon. That could change how teams operate — and, eventually, how much money teams are allowed to spend, or even forced to spend. There are a ton of unknown variables at this point. What we do know (for the most part) are which stars will be available to sign when the market does open up. From Los Angeles Dodgers ace Tarik Skubal to top Japanese free agent Teruaki Sato, here are the 10 best free agents (according t
item.content:encoded:
MLB free agency takes on a new urgency this winter with a Dec. 1 lockout on the horizon. That could change how teams operate — and, eventually, how much money teams are allowed to spend, or even forced to spend. There are a ton of unknown variables at this point.
What we do know (for the most part) are which stars will be available to sign when the market does open up. From Los Angeles Dodgers ace Tarik Skubal to top Japanese free agent Teruaki Sato, here are the 10 best free agents (according to FanSided's Robert Murray) with projected contracts and destinations.
LHP Tarik Skubal
Projected deal: 9 years, $378 million ($42 million AAV) with New York Mets
Regardless of how CBA negotiations shake out, Tarik Skubal's long-rumored $400 million price tag may ultimately prove to be an overestimation. There's a reason no pitcher has ever received such a paycheck, Shohei Ohtani notwithstanding. Still, Skubal should become the highest-paid pitcher in MLB history. His durability, both in-game and season-long, combined with razor-sharp stuff in the prime of his career, should give teams the confidence to invest in Skubal over an extended period.
The Dodgers are the natural landing spot after acquiring him at the trade deadline, but the Mets are baseball's richest team and there's mounting pressure for New York to start competing, in a serious way, with Juan Soto and Francisco Lindor. Skubal is the ultimate floor-raiser in a rotation, and he'd form a mean one-two punch with breakout ace Nolan McLean.
OF Seiya Suzuki
Projected deal: 4 years, $100 million ($25 million AAV) with Toronto Blue Jays
Seiya Suzuki is probably the best bat available in free agency. The 32-year-old outfielder has been a model of consistency for the Cubs, with at least 20 home runs and an .800-plus OPS in three straight seasons. He's a plus defender in right field, too, where he posted career-best metrics in 2026. Suzuki has a rocket-like arm and consistently holds runners from the back corner.
Plenty of teams will take an interest in Suzuki's right-handed power profile; he draws walks and operates with sage discipline in the batter's box, despite occasionally elevated strikeout numbers. In the end, Toronto represents the most logical intersection of need and financial firepower to outbid the field.
OF Randy Arozarena
Projected deal: 5 years, $110 million ($22 million AAV) with Philadelphia Phillies
Randy Arozarena set new career highs in average (.281), OPS (.865) and home runs (26) in his walk year, emerging as one of the few bright spots on an otherwise disappointing Mariners team. He's more adequate than exceptional with his glove, but Arozarena provides middle-order power and he's a great personality hire.
The Phillies need Arozarena's bat and competitive fire in equal measure, plus he can help to safely return Bryce Harper to first base next season. Philadelphia desperately needs a right-handed slugger behind Harper in the lineup; the ability to finally add some stability to the outfield depth chart, as opposed to a 2026 rewind of the Adolis García or Max Kepler situations, should greatly appeal to a desperate Dave Dombrowski.
3B Teruaki Sato
Projected deal: 3 years, $75 million ($25 million AAV) with New York Yankees
Teruaki Sato is the most accomplished international free agent hoping to come Stateside this offseason. An MVP candidate in Japan's NPB, Sato hit .306 this year with 39 home runs and a .991 OPS. There are swing-and-miss and defense concerns, not dissimilar to the vague uncertainties that tanked Munetaka Murakami's stock last winter. Murakami ended up on a two-year deal with the White Sox, which he immediately outperformed.
Sato's left-handed power and upside at 27 years old could mean his market flourishes. But, given the baked-in gambles that come with signing an international free agent, he could end up getting lowballed, much like Murakami. A three-year, $75 million contract gives Sato a nice payday upfront while still hedging against potential struggles with a short-term framework. The Yankees need an infield slugger and have the money to roll the dice, so to speak, on Sato's immense talent.
LHP Trevor Rogers
Projected deal: 3 years, $60 million ($20 million) with Baltimore Orioles
Trevor Rogers has dealt with his share of injuries and inconsistency over the years, but he's coming off of two strong campaigns in Baltimore — and he's only 28 years old, so there's room left to establish himself as more than a third or fourth starter type. He couldn't recapture the success of 2025, when Rogers returned from injury to post a 1.81 ERA in 18 starts, but his 4.03 ERA last season does not capture the strength of his stuff (3.60 xERA). Moreover, the career-high 30 starts and 169.2 innings pitched was a nice addition to his résumé.
Teams will probably balk at dropping a full bag on Rogers' doorstep, ultimately, which opens the door for a short-term contract (probably with an opt-out clause or two) and a return to Baltimore. The Orioles need pitching badly and there are precious few better options than Rogers floating around the open market. This contract could turn into a total bargain.
RHP Freddy Peralta
Projected deal: 4 years, $84 million ($21 million AAV) with Chicago Cubs
Freddy Peralta's walk year has been a roller coaster of emotions. He bombed in New York after the Mets dealt multiple top-100 prospects to acquire him in an offseason trade. Then, after relocating to Tampa at the trade deadline, Peralta started slow before gradually picking up steam in September. Down the stretch and into the playoffs, he has looked more like the Cy Young candidate we witnessed in Milwaukee last season.
Peralta has not made the strongest case to prospective suitors in 2026, so a one-year, high-AAV deal to "prove it" is on the table. Ultimately, however, the 30-year-old should still be able to coax a substantial multi-year offer out of a desperate contender. His longtime NL Central rivals, the Cubs, are one such desperate contender. Peralta could join with the now-healthy Cade Horton and Justin Steele to revitalize Chicago's World Series hopes for 2027.
C Ryan Jeffers
Projected deal: 4 years, $68 million ($17 million AAV) with Minnesota Twins
The catcher market is tough to project, as there are so few who can hit like Ryan Jeffers. He was excellent in Minnesota this season, with 14 home runs and an .814 OPS in roughly half a season. He's the best catcher on the market, but Jeffers is not exactly lauded for his defense nor his game management behind the plate. He is not without injury concerns either, while even the best catchers end up in a timeshare eventually (especially when, like Jeffers, their glovework can be problematic).
Since there is such an absence of reliable hitters at the catcher position, Jeffers should be able to land a solid multi-year deal in the middle of his prime. A return to the Twins should not be discounted, even with Eduardo Tait and Vahn Lackey coming up through the Minors on accelerated timelines. Minnesota made a conscious decision not to trade him at the deadline, after all. The Twins would probably like to compete next season.
RHP Michael King
Projected deal: five years, $120 million ($24 million AAV) with San Diego Padres
Michael King returned to San Diego last winter on a backloaded three-year deal with opt outs. After an excellent showing in the playoffs, he will probably axe the remaining two years and $66 million on that contract in hopes of securing more guaranteed money this winter. King is not the sexiest name on the pitching market by any stretch, but he has made himself into a dependable workhorse with October equity.
The Padres clearly love King and new ownership, with their stated intention to build a contender, will probably consent to a reworked contract. San Diego has a paper-thin rotation as is. Losing King without a viable alternative in place could be disastrous, as the Padres don't have the trade ammo to compensate for a free agency exodus.
2B Brandon Lowe
Projected deal: 3 years, $66 million ($22 million AAV) with Pittsburgh Pirates
Brandon Lowe arrived in Pittsburgh via offseason trade and immediately became the most bankable presence in their lineup, with 35 home runs, 96 RBI and an .824 OPS. The 32-year-old can get in trouble with swing-and-miss, but he's a slugging outlier at second base. Moreover, Lowe quietly posted some of the best defensive metrics in MLB last season after struggling for years on the defensive end. It's fair to be skeptical about Lowe's ability to sustain this elite defense into his mid-30s, but he did everything he could to maximize his value as a free agent.
To that point, it's hard to imagine the Pirates letting Lowe walk without a fight. Pittsburgh threw more money around last offseason, with the front office clearly committed to changing their postseason fortunes. It did not come together in 2026, but Pittsburgh has a dangerous lineup and a very talented pitching staff. There's potential for a breakthrough in 2027, especially if Lowe sticks around.
LHP Adrián Morejón
Projected deal: 4 years, $68 million ($17 million AAV) with Toronto Blue Jays
Adrián Morejón's mystery-shrouded absence in San Diego's NLDS loss to Milwaukee was a tough pill to swallow, but once again, the Padres end the season feeling like the second-best team in the National League. They were able to at least put a scare into the Brewers where even the Dodgers could not. Part of the reason for San Diego's success this season, despite dramatic fluctuations from their lineup, was an elite bullpen. Morejón was only the setup man to Mason Miller, but the 27-year-old southpaw is still among the best relievers in baseball.
Over the past three seasons, Morejón has a 2.58 ERA with 248 strikeouts in 223.1 innings. It's hard to find a more steadfast high-leverage arm, especially one as young as Morejón. He could get some real length on his contract in a reliever-needy marketplace. The Blue Jays figure to be as aggressive as any team this offseason; Morejón setting up Louis Varland, with Tyler Rogers and Spencer Miles to cover other late-inning spots, is a tantalizing proposition.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees had another very strong regular season where they went 93-68 in 161 games.
That said, they also had another letdown in the MLB playoffs when they got swept by the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS.
In addition, the Yankees also lost the final game on their home field in the Bronx.
Yankees Star Makes 6-Word Aaron Boone Statement
With their season over, a lot of blame has been placed on manager Aaron Boone.
They have only been able to reach the World Series one time over his nine-year stint as manager.
In a recent interview with Michael Kay (via The Michael Kay Show), José Caballero was asked about Boone.
Kay: “Did you like playing for Aaron Boone?”
Caballero: “Hey, I like playing for him. I like playing for the Yankees. I think we are, like I say, a complete team that we could do way better than what we did. And like I said, I think there’s no one else to blame than us as players. We were in there, we the ones making plays and hitting the ball.”
Looking At Boone
Manager Aaron Boone #17 of the New York Yankees walks out to the mound during the fifth inning against the Tampa Bay Rays in game two of the American League Division Series at Tropicana Field on October 05, 2026 in St Petersburg, Florida.
Boone took over the Yankees in 2018.
They have made the MLB playoffs in eight out of his nine seasons (and reached Game 5 of the 2024 World Series).
The Yankees wrote (via X) on February 20, 2025: “The New York Yankees today announced that they have signed Manager Aaron Boone to a two-year contract extension through the 2027 season.”
Looking At Caballero
Jose Caballero #72 of the New York Yankees reacts following his eighth inning three-run home run against the Boston Red Sox at Yankee Stadium on August 30, 2026 in New York City.
Caballero has been in the MLB for four seasons.
He spent the first year of his career with the Seattle Mariners.
Following Seattle, Caballero played part of two seasons for the Rays.
MLB.com wrote (on July 31, 2025): “Tampa Bay Rays traded SS José Caballero to New York Yankees for CF Everson Pereira and Future Considerations. Player To Be Named Later or Cash Considerations.”

item.content:encoded:
CLEVELAND –- José Ramírez se retirará entre los líderes en muchos departamentos de por vida en los Guardianes. De hecho, ya está primero en partidos jugados (1,734) y extrabases (765), más segundo en jonrones (297) – entre muchas cifras destacadas en la historia de la franquicia.
El sábado en el Juego 4 de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Americana, el dominicano empató un récord de Cleveland de más partidos consecutivos embasándose en la postemporada con 16, desde el 2024. El jardinero Steven Kwam tenía el récord, que ahora comparte con Ramírez, al hacer lo mismo entre el 2022 y el 2024.
“Mr. Lapara”, llegó el sábado a 16 juegos consecutivos embasándose en playoffs al negociar una base por bolas ante su compatriota y derecho de los Rays, Freddy Peralta, quien había entrado al partido como relevista. En total, Ramírez ha participado en ocho postemporadas con los Guardianes, también una marca de todos los tiempos del equipo.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Kyle Tucker sends promising message to Dodgers fans after atrocious debut season
item.dc:creator: Valentina Martinez
item.description: The Dodgers face several questions after an early postseason exit in the National League Championship Series. The dynasty that the Dodgers have put together is in jeopardy of ending within the next few seasons if the front office can't assemble another winning roster. Kyle Tucker, who was signed to a four-year, $240 million deal ahead of the 2026 season, addressed fans as the future of the franchise is in limbo. "Through every high and low, thank you to our fans for riding with us all season. We
item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers face several questions after an early postseason exit in the National League Championship Series.
The dynasty that the Dodgers have put together is in jeopardy of ending within the next few seasons if the front office can't assemble another winning roster. Kyle Tucker, who was signed to a four-year, $240 million deal ahead of the 2026 season, addressed fans as the future of the franchise is in limbo.
"Through every high and low, thank you to our fans for riding with us all season. We appreciate the love and support more than you know. This isn't the end — we'll be back," Tucker wrote in an Instagram post.
For most of 2026, the four-time All-Star was far from full form. Tucker ended the regular season with a .233 batting average, 17 home runs and 70 RBIs. He entered October with a .715 OPS, the lowest mark since his debut season in 2018 when he played 28 games.
Tucker's struggles became a point of contention among the fan base, but the star outfielder came to life in the postseason. The 29-year-old averaged .333 with a .967 OPS in October, which was perhaps the only highlight of his inaugural Dodgers season.
The Dodgers, who face an uncertain future after the failed quest for a three-peat, will need Tucker to play at All-Star strength the entire 2027 season as one of the many veterans on the roster. While Tucker's performance next year can't be known, one thing is certain, the Dodgers will surely try to get younger this winter.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Padres Predicted to Land Tarik Skubal in Blockbuster Offseason Move
item.dc:creator: Matt Levine
item.description: The San Diego Padres were able to get into the playoffs after what was a shaky start to the 2026 MLB season, but the team fell short of its goal to win the World Series. San Diego lost in four games to the Milwaukee Brewers, seeing another year go by without a title, sending this team into a crucial offseason. The Padres' front office will have a lot to figure out this offseason, especially within the starting rotation, with key players hitting free agency. Padres Linked With Tarik Skubal One na
item.content:encoded:
The San Diego Padres were able to get into the playoffs after what was a shaky start to the 2026 MLB season, but the team fell short of its goal to win the World Series.
San Diego lost in four games to the Milwaukee Brewers, seeing another year go by without a title, sending this team into a crucial offseason. The Padres' front office will have a lot to figure out this offseason, especially within the starting rotation, with key players hitting free agency.
Padres Linked With Tarik Skubal
One name that has started to generate some buzz around the Padres as the offseason gets going is ace Tarik Skubal, who split time with the Los Angeles Dodgers and Detroit Tigers. San Diego could look to go after Skubal, giving their rotation a major boost for the future.
MLB analyst Zachary D. Rymer of Bleacher Report recently ranked landing spots for Skubal in a new piece. Within this, Rymer listed the Padres as a top landing spot, and the fit does make a lot of sense.
"If ever there was a way to show they mean business, it's by signing Skubal away from those darn Dodgers. Maybe it wouldn't totally undo the little brother vs. big brother dynamic between the two NL West powers, but it would give the Padres a real trump card: the best pitcher in baseball.
"Besides, the Padres are going to need Skubal if Michael King declines his $28 million player option for 2027 and becomes a free agent. Skubal is one of the few pitchers in MLB who would represent an upgrade over King, even if signing him would likely cost more than $40 million per year," Rymer wrote.
The Padres have spent a lot of money in the last few offseasons, which has backfired on this franchise at times. It has seen the team allow multiple stars to leave town, pushing back what the ceiling of this organization could be.
Skubal could change the entire starting rotation for the Padres this offseason, but he is expected to receive a deal over $300 million, if not closer to $400 million. San Diego has given out large contracts in the past, but this would be a new precedent for this team.
Should the Padres Go After Tarik Skubal?
On the field, the Padres should absolutely do whatever it takes to bring Skubal to San Diego. But the money is will be another question that this organization is going to have to grapple with.
With the new ownership in place, the Padres are expected to keep spending, but giving Skubal what he wants could be tough. San Diego has a lot of heavy contracts on the books already, and handing out another could be a big swing for this team.
Overall, the Padres will be involved in the Skubal sweepstakes, especially with how president of baseball operations A.J. Preller operates. Nobody can count out San Diego in this process, but other teams could present an easier path to give the lefty ace the type of deal that he is looking for this winter.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Padres Predicted to Land Tarik Skubal in Blockbuster Offseason Move appeared first on HEAVY.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox's lefty-dominated starting rotation is expected to lose its only righty and its ace. Sonny Gray will take to the free agent market after he posted one of the best seasons of his career at age 36.
Gray has a mutual option on his contract, but those are rarely triggered. He and the Red Sox have to agree on his pay and $30 million is likely more than the front office is willing to commit for one year of the 37 year old Gray.
A reunion isn't completely off the table, though. Gray was discouraged with Red Sox manager Chad Tracy's to pull him in the fifth inning of Wild Card Game 2, but he has seemingly put that aside and mentioned Boston as a potential future destination when speaking about winning a championship before he retires (subscription required).
There are still some possible obstacles to a reunion between Gray and the Sox, though. MLB insider Mark Feinsand reports that the Red Sox will be among Gray's "primary suitors" this offseason, but some believe he might want to play for a team closer to his home in Tennessee.
MLB insider Mark Feinsand believes geography may come between Red Sox-Sonny Gray reunion
That belief makes sense, given the way Gray framed his comments on his potential retirement — he said he would be done with baseball "in a heartbeat" if his family wanted him to be. Proximity to them is obviously important to the veteran.
It is promising that the Red Sox are expected to be one of the teams pursuing Gray most aggressively. He was one of the best pitchers in the American League last season, likely to finish in or near the top five in Cy Young Award voting, and none of the righties the Red Sox already have are quite as promising. Brayan Bello had one of the strangest, up-and-down years we'll ever see and there's no guarantee of his performance next year. Tanner Houck and Kutter Crawford were injured all season and their futures are just as clouded.
If Gray is hoping to play his final seasons closer to his home, the Atlanta Braves could be dangerous competition in his market. Righty Tyler Mahle will be a free agent. Spencer Strider dealt with elbow inflammation for much of last season and he's regressed from his early career success. Spencer Schwellenbach missed the entire 2026 season due to injury. Given their 2026 performances, Gray might think he has a better chance of winning a championship with the Braves than with the Red Sox, furthering Atlanta's potential as a top suitor.
While improving the offense should undoubtedly be Boston's No. 1 priority this offseason, reuniting with Gray would be an undeniable boost to its rotation. If the Red Sox hope to keep him Gray in the northeast for another year or two, they'll have to outbid and outperform suitors local to Tennessee this winter.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees Center Field Dilemma Points To Oneil Cruz Trade
item.dc:creator: Pete Altomaro
item.description: The New York Yankees enter this offseason with a glaring hole in center field that free agency will not fill. The front office needs a solution now, but the available names on the market look weak. According to Yahoo Sports, the team simply does not have many options to sign as free agents. item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees enter this offseason with a glaring hole in center field that free agency will not fill. The front office needs a solution now, but the available names on the market look weak. According to Yahoo Sports, the team simply does not have many options to sign as free agents. This reality forces the club to look elsewhere for help.
Internal fixes have failed to work over the last two years. Austin Wells at catcher for example has shown great skills with his glove, but his bat has struggled to find a rhythm. The team also tried rookie Spencer Jones, who looked fresh but posted a minus-4 Outs Above Average metric in center field. That number was only a slight improvement over the minus-6 mark recorded by veteran Trent Grisham. Per Yahoo Sports, the defensive regression at this key position has become a major problem for the roster.
The Free Agent Trap
Most teams would look to the open market to fix a defensive gap. The Yankees cannot do that this time. The best available players come with heavy baggage. Daulton Varsho cannot hit well enough to justify the cost, and Luis Robert Jr. is known for being injury-prone while also lacking consistent offense. Even if Grisham returns, he should only play a corner spot, not center. Reports note that his glove has regressed since his bat finally improved in New York.
This lack of viable names means the Yankees must be creative. They cannot just wait for a deal to happen. The team needs to make a move that others might think is too risky. A trade is the only way to get a player who can actually play center field every day.
The Cruz Connection
Oneil Cruz stands out as the most logical target for this difficult task. He is a charismatic left-handed hitter who was named after Paul O'Neill. The Yankees have been linked to Cruz for years, with reports dating back to the summer of 2025. Nothing came of those talks then, but the interest never really went away. Yahoo Sports reports that the front office has targeted Cruz for a minimum of two years.
Getting him will not be easy. Reports suggest that the Pittsburgh Pirates might require some serious prying to part ways with their star. The Yankees have the assets to make a deal work, but they must act fast. Waiting too long could let another team step in and claim him. The clock is ticking on this specific opportunity to fix the roster.
Historical Context
The need for a true center fielder is not new for this franchise. Brett Gardner was probably the best the team had in the last 20 years before he retired after the 2021 season. A dropped fly ball during Game 5 of the 2024 World Series ended center field duties for Aaron Judge, despite his status as an elite player. The team has tried many names, but none have solved the issue for a full season.

カブスからフリーエージェント（FA）となった今永昇太投手が、早くも2027年シーズンに向けて始動した。米国のアスリート向けトレーニング施設「Cressey Sports Performance（CSP）」が13日（日本時間14日）、YouTubeで動画を公開。フロリダの施設でトレーニングを行った今永の様子を伝えている。
■熱心にディスカッションする姿も
CSPは、アスリートのトレーニングやパフォーマンス向上を専門とする施設で、野球選手の投球や打撃の分析も行っている。今永は2025年10月にも同施設を訪れ、投球分析を実施。MLB公式サイトが当時の取り組みを報じた。そして今回、CSPの創業者エリック・クレッシー氏が自身のYouTubeチャンネルで動画を公開。今永のトレーニングの様子を伝えている。
今回の訪問では、投球時の身体の動きを捉える「モーションキャプチャー」や地面にかかる力を計測する「フォースプレート」、さらにボールを握る際のグリップ圧を測定する機器などを使用。CSPは「収集したデータを2027年に向けたトレーニングや投球プランの作成に活用する」と説明している。
今季の今永は32試合に先発し、11勝10敗、防御率3.77を記録。ポストシーズンでは登板機会が訪れることなくチームは敗れ去った。来季の所属先は決まっていないが、すでに新たなシーズンを見据えて動き始めている。

item.title: [southsideshowdown.com] 1 dream target, 1 realistic target, 1 mistake White Sox could make in offseason pitching search
item.dc:creator: Noah Phalen

Getz reflected on the season and provided some updates on the future. item.content:encoded:
Earlier this week, White Sox GM Chris Getz spoke to the media for the first time since Chicago’s ALDS Game 5 loss against the Guardians. Getz reflected on the season and provided some updates on the future. Among the topics of conversation were positions the White Sox will pursue upgrades in during the upcoming offseason, with Getz emphasizing the starting rotation as an obvious area of need. I previously discussed a few starting pitching options I’d like to see the White Sox pursue, so this will be a bit of a different conversation. Let’s discuss a dream target, a realistic target, and a mistake the White Sox could make in their pitching search.
Dream Target: LHP Tarik Skubal
It’s impossible to discuss the pitching free agent class without mentioning two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, the best pitcher available by a wide margin and one of the most dominant arms in all of baseball. The soon-to-be 30-year-old spent the first six and a half seasons with the Tigers before a midseason trade sent him to the Dodgers. He won the Cy Young Award in both 2024 and 2025, with a 2.39 and 2.21 ERA in each year, and would’ve been squarely in the mix for 2026 as well if not for an injury that cost him six weeks in May and June.
Do I think the White Sox have any chance at landing Tarik Skubal? Probably not. To be honest, I’d be surprised if they’re even interested. But Chicago has a very low payroll and an obvious need in the starting rotation. In theory, they could add Skubal for $30-40 million a year and still have payroll room for other upgrades on the roster. They’re a young, exciting team who seems to be just beginning their competitive window, so it’s a destination that could be appealing for Skubal. He’ll no doubt have his pick though, and it’s hard to see the White Sox competing financially with some of the other markets. I guess one can dream.
Realistic Target: RHP Tyler Mahle
Maybe big-game hunting isn’t realistic for the White Sox this offseason, but there’s no reason they can’t add at least one impact starting pitcher in free agency. Braves righty Tyler Mahle is an interesting veteran arm who shined during the second half of the season and into the playoffs. While most pitchers traded at the deadline struggled in their new home, Mahle posted a 1.99 ERA in nine starts with Atlanta and allowed just two earned runs in 13.1 innings in the Postseason. Mahle turned 32 in September and will be looking to leverage his strong finish into a solid contract. Perhaps a two or three-year deal could be in the cards for a player who’s always had a productive career but has battled frequent injuries. Mahle would be a strong veteran presence in the White Sox rotation and has a recent history of Postseason success. He could be one of the names on Chicago’s target list.
Mistake: LHP Robbie Ray
Left-hander Robbie Ray was one of the most talked about names ahead of the trade deadline, and the Giants ultimately dealt him within their division to the San Diego Padres. Some concerning metrics made Ray a prime candidate for regression, and he posted just a 5.02 ERA in nine starts for San Diego down the stretch. Still, he has back to back seasons with an ERA under 3.70, so he’s deserving of a big league deal this offseason. I don’t think that should be the White Sox, however. Ray is now 35 years old and his underlying metrics were scary in 2026. He pitched in two ballparks that heavily favor pitchers, whereas Chicago is a more hitter-friendly environment. Ray is a veteran who has struggled in the playoffs in his career, and his age is a real concern. I’d stay away here if I were the White Sox.

item.title: [fansided.com] The stars are aligning for the Mets to sign Tarik Skubal, with one giant asterisk standing in their way
item.dc:creator: Zachary Rotman

I know, this seems crazy. Why would Skubal want to join a Mets team that just won 74 games in 2026 and has failed to make the playoffs in each of Juan Soto's two years in Flushing? Well, here's a look at why the Mets make more sense for Skubal than you might think, and what might
item.content:encoded:
The offseason is a perfect time for New York Mets fans like myself to be optimistic, and that's exactly what I'm going to be doing here when I say the stars are aligning for the Mets to sign Tarik Skubal in free agency. I know, this seems crazy. Why would Skubal want to join a Mets team that just won 74 games in 2026 and has failed to make the playoffs in each of Juan Soto's two years in Flushing?
Well, here's a look at why the Mets make more sense for Skubal than you might think, and what might stand in their way of making this dream of arguably the best pitcher in the sport playing out the rest of his prime in Queens a reality.
The Dodgers' lack of aggression might play into the Mets' hands
When the Los Angeles Dodgers traded for Tarik Skubal, MLB fans not only assumed they'd automatically win a World Series title, but they also assumed that the Dodgers would easily extend Skubal, given their recent history of spending on star-level talent. It's absolutely possible that the Dodgers do choose to re-sign Skubal, but look at what ESPN's Alden Gonzalez had to say about that.
"Skubal's agent, Scott Boras, will probably want to get something done with his client before the lockout, but it would be really difficult for the Dodgers to justify signing Skubal to a massive deal before knowing what MLB's economic model will look like," Gonzalez wrote. "If there is a cap-and-floor system in the next collective bargaining agreement, there will be some sort of phase-in period. But it will undoubtedly impact the Dodgers in the near future. It would be a major risk to sign Skubal before knowing what they're signing up for."
To sum up, Gonzalez is predicting that Skubal's agent, Scott Boras, will likely want to get a deal done with his top client before the expected lockout at the beginning of December, but the Dodgers would want to wait until after the lockout so they know what the economic model of the sport will look like. This makes a ton of sense, given the massive amount of money they've already committed to 2027 and beyond. It's worth noting that this is just Gonzalez's belief, and not a sourced report.
If the Dodgers won't aggressively pursue Skubal before December 1, why can't the Mets be the team to give him an offer he can't refuse? It's not like the Mets haven't been in this position before.
The Mets have beaten the competition to the punch pre-lockout before
Just like a lockout is looming this offseason, one loomed back in the 2021 offseason, when Max Scherzer was a free agent. Scherzer, who was represented by Scott Boras, made it clear that he wanted to sign before the league locked the players out, and he did just that, coming to terms on a three-year, $130 milllion deal with, guess who, the New York Mets.
Now, say what you want about how the deal aged (Scherzer pitched brilliantly in 2022 but struggled in that year's postseason and was traded at the 2023 trade deadline), but the Mets beat the Dodgers and a couple of other teams to the punch to sign the future Hall of Famer on a deal that paid him well over $40 million annually.
Can't that history repeat itself? The Mets won the Scherzer sweepstakes not because they were some powerhouse, but because the Dodgers didn't want to go above and beyond to sign him as the Mets did. Reports suggest Skubal would like to sign pre-lockout and the Dodgers don't want to go above and beyond. Why can't the Mets do what they've already done and give their fan base something to get excited about before the lockout?
If the Dodgers and Mets won't pay Tarik Skubal, what team will?
Let's just assume that both the Dodgers and the Mets decide that paying Skubal is not in their best interest. Is there another team out there willing to spend the $300-to-$400 million on Skubal that he'll likely be asking for?
The New York Yankees are often willing spenders, but with a ton of money invested in starting pitchers like Gerrit Cole, Max Fried and Carlos Rodon, would they pay Skubal before addressing their offense? The Philadelphia Phillies should be eager to spend after another early elimination, but again, is paying on pitching in their best interest? The Chicago Cubs could certainly use the pitching, but they've never even handed out a $200 million contract. Would they give $300+ million to Skubal? The Toronto Blue Jays have the money and the need for pitching help, but they also just paid Dylan Cease handsomely last winter and finished last in runs scored this past season. A return to the Detroit Tigers would be awesome, but that feels unrealistic.
There're other teams like the San Francisco Giants and the Los Angeles Angels who might show interest, but again, there isn't really a perfect fit. If the Mets and Dodgers won't meet an outlandish asking price, which team will?
The Mets have a clear need for a high-end starting pitcher
The Mets are building a strong rotation, with youngsters like Nolan McLean, Christian Scott and Zac Thornton in the fold, but the team lacks a true ace. They hoped Freddy Peralta would fill that void when they acquired him from the Brewers in the 2025 offseason, but that experiment flopped spectacularly.
It's hard to see Skubal flopping, though, at least in 2027. He remains one of, if not the best pitcher in the sport, and even after an early-season injury scare, Skubal ended his season with a 2.72 ERA in 26 starts. He's as dynamic as they come, and would instantly make the Mets true postseason contenders.
If they don't sign Skubal, who else could they realistically get? The next-best options, such as Michael King, Kevin Gausman and Clay Holmes, aren't exactly aces. They could potentially swing a trade, but doing so is easier said than done. It feels like Skubal or bust when it comes to getting a bona fide ace.
Would David Stearns be willing to abandon his starting pitching philosophy to sign Tarik Skubal?
We know that the Mets have the need, the money and the location necessary to lure Skubal to the team, but would the individual responsible for making such a move, David Stearns, be willing to do so? Stearns has famously been averse to handing massive deals to starting pitchers, passing on guys like Corbin Burnes, Max Fried and Dylan Cease, to name a few, and instead relying on shorter-term gambles.
Most of these have not paid off, which is partially why the Mets have missed the playoffs in back-to-back years, but will there be a mindset shift? Will Stearns suddenly go from a guy unwilling to offer more than three years to a pitcher over the age of 30 to willing to meet Skubal's demands?
That's an answer we're soon going to learn the answer to, and it could be the difference in Skubal joining the Mets or signing elsewhere. If Stearns is all in, the stars feel like they're aligning for something special to happen.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] The Philadelphia Phillies Don't Actually Need Tarik Skubal
item.dc:creator: Matthew Schmidt
item.description: The Philadelphia Phillies absolutely need to bolster their roster this offseason after yet another early playoff exit, but they actually shouldn't be pursuing the biggest fish on the free-agent market. Tarik Skubal is going to be the top player available this winter, and he will surely have a wide range of suitors. But the Phillies should not be one of them. Why? item.content:encoded:
The Philadelphia Phillies absolutely need to bolster their roster this offseason after yet another early playoff exit, but they actually shouldn't be pursuing the biggest fish on the free-agent market.
Tarik Skubal is going to be the top player available this winter, and he will surely have a wide range of suitors. But the Phillies should not be one of them.
Why? Because Philadelphia already boasts one of the best starting rotations in baseball.
The trio of Cristopher Sanchez, Jesus Luzardo and Zack Wheeler is fantastic, and Andrew Painter showed tremendous signs during the second half of the season.
Yes, Aaron Nola is infinitely replaceable, but he did have a strong second half overall, even if his last couple of starts were less than desirable.
Skubal is likely to command $400 million. He's one of the best pitchers in baseball, he's a left-hander and his agent is Scott Boras.
The Phillies have already been monitoring their payroll closely as it is. Their roster is littered with lucrative long-term deals, some of which are not exactly good ones. Do they really want to spend nearly half a billion dollars in an area that doesn't have a need?
Philadelphia needs bats and it needs relievers; period. The Phillies had one of the worst offenses in the league this year, and their bullpen was a disaster down the stretch — and really, for most of the campaign.
That is where Philadelphia should be spending its money.
Sure, the idea of Skubal is tempting. He is a dominant force who won back-to-back Cy Young awards in 2024 and 2025 and just posted a 2.72 ERA and 0.964 WHIP in 2026.
But he's also turning 30 years old next month and has had multiple elbow surgeries. Handing him big-time money over an extended period of time is going to be a significant risk, and it's one that the Phillies really can't take.
Philadelphia's holes are obvious. It must address its outfield, which didn't field a single reliable hitter this season. It needs to find another bat either at second base or third base, depending on where the Phillies want to put Bryson Stott. And they also need to bring in a serviceable catcher alongside J.T. Realmuto.
And of course, it must build a better bridge to Jhoan Duran in the ninth inning.
Skubal does not fill any of those needs. At that cost, it's simply not worth it.

item.title: [Jays Journal] Randy Arozarena’s East Coast preference could put the Blue Jays in the free-agent race

item.content:encoded:
Randy Arozarena’s reported preference to return to the East Coast should immediately grab the attention of the Toronto Blue Jays. The free-agent outfielder makes his home in Tampa, trains in Florida and, according to reports, would prefer to join an eastern team that holds spring training in that state. Toronto can offer each of those things through its Florida base in Dunedin.
More importantly, the Blue Jays can offer Arozarena an obvious role for 2027 and beyond. Their outfield picture has a lot of uncertainty heading into next year, and the lineup needs precisely what he provides: a right-handed hitter with consistent power, strong on-base skills and enough speed to create pressure once he reaches base.
Randy Arozarena fills several Blue Jays needs at once
Arozarena is coming off the most productive season of his career. He hit .281/.381/.484 with 26 home runs, 79 RBI and 113 runs across 154 games for Seattle, good for an .865 OPS and a 151 wRC+. His 5.5 FanGraphs WAR placed him among the game’s most valuable position players, while his 10.1 per cent walk rate proved he wasn't just swinging for the fences every time up.
The Blue Jays’ current outfield options lean heavily to the left side, with Nathan Lukes, Addison Barger, and Brett Bateman the likely every day guys all hit from the left side. Prospects such as Sean Keys (though limited in the outfield) and Yohendrick Piñango also bat left-handed. Anthony Santander is a switch-hitter but has struggled to stay healthy, while Davis Schneider’s roster status is uncertain at the moment pending the non-tender deadline / arbitration process.
Arozarena would give manager John Schneider a proven right-handed threat that could slot immediately into left-field on an every day basis. And he'd need that bat in there considering how consistent he's been as a slugger over his MLB career. Arozarena has hit at-least 20 home runs in every full season since 2021.
Then there is the speed. Arozarena stole 26 bases in 2026 and has reached the 20-steal mark in six consecutive seasons. Pairing him near the top of the order with Bateman would give the Blue Jays a mix of contact, on-base ability and baserunning they largely lacked outside of Andrés Giménez and Bateman later in the season. Arozarena as a number two hitter behind Bateman could be an immediate recipe for success.
While may no longer be a standout defender in left field, his offence and baserunning would address enough weaknesses to make that trade-off manageable. The other complication lies in the fact that Arozarena could cost the Blue Jays more than just the dollar value he signs.
Arozarena will likely get a one-year qualifying offer from Seattle which is expected to be worth $23.15 million. He would likely reject it in search of a multiyear contract which would then cost the Blue Jays a draft pick. At least, that's how the current system works. If Toronto waits until after the new CBA is signed, that entire structure could change.
But they might not want to wait it out too long. Arozarena’s geographic preference helps the Blue Jays, but it hardly makes Toronto the favourite. The New York Yankees should have many of the same reasons to pursue him. They could move Cody Bellinger out of left field and install Arozarena as another right-handed power bat around Aaron Judge.
Boston also looms as a natural bidder, particularly given Arozarena’s history in the AL East and his career success at Fenway Park. Any market that includes multiple wealthy division rivals could push the contract beyond Toronto’s comfort zone, especially for a player who turns 32 in February.
While Arozarena is not a flawless target and his age creates some risk on a long-term deal, the top of the free agent class is not loaded with stars this winter. The Blue Jays need right-handed power in the outfield and Arozarena has proven he can provide that over his career. The fit makes a ton of sense on paper - whether it comes to fruition or not remains to be seen.

item.title: [Chicago Tribune] Milwaukee Brewers’ NLCS sweep means 2 of MLB’s lower spenders will meet in World Series for 1st time since ’91
item.dc:creator: Ronald Blum
item.description: NEW YORK — When the Milwaukee Brewers defeated the mighty, monied Los Angeles Dodgers on Thursday night, they set up the first World Series between two of baseball’s smaller spenders in 35 years — just as team owners are arguing that clubs such as the Brewers need a salary cap to compete consistently. The Brewers will face the Cleveland Guardians or Tampa Bay Rays in a best-of-seven Series for the title beginning Friday, ensuring two clubs in the bottom half of big-league payrolls will play in t
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — When the Milwaukee Brewers defeated the mighty, monied Los Angeles Dodgers on Thursday night, they set up the first World Series between two of baseball’s smaller spenders in 35 years — just as team owners are arguing that clubs such as the Brewers need a salary cap to compete consistently.
The Brewers will face the Cleveland Guardians or Tampa Bay Rays in a best-of-seven Series for the title beginning Friday, ensuring two clubs in the bottom half of big-league payrolls will play in the World Series for the first time since 1991. The Dodgers, New York Mets and New York Yankees will watch from home with payrolls this season that each cost more than the Brewers, Guardians and Rays rosters combined.
The low-budget World Series showdown will start six weeks before a likely management lockout, a work stoppage that threatens the 2027 season as owners and players battle over the sport’s lack of a salary cap.
Speaking at the All-Star Game in July, MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred made his case for a cap while saying exceptions did not reflect parity.
“Our view of the world is that over a very long period of time there’s a very strong relationship between who gets into the playoffs and who proceeds, notwithstanding the exceptions we’ve got,” he said.
The Brewers, who won the NL pennant with a four-game sweep of the Dodgers, had MLB’s 19th-highest payroll as of Aug. 31, while the Rays were 25th and Guardians 30th. The last time both pennant winners were among the bottom 50% in player spending was when the Minnesota Twins (15th among 26 teams) beat the Atlanta Braves (19th) for the 1991 championship.
In terms of market size, Milwaukee ranks as MLB’s 30th and smallest Designated Market Area, defined by Nielsen as non-overlapping geographic regions that group counties based on television viewing areas. Cleveland is 22nd and Tampa, Fla., 15th.
If the Guardians win the AL pennant, this would mark the first World Series involving two teams in the bottom half of MLB cities by DMA since the St. Louis Cardinals (24th) beat the Detroit Tigers (18th) in 2006. No small-market team has won the World Series since the Kansas City Royals in 2015.
Three years after the Twins won that 1991 title, players went on strike as owners pushed for a salary cap, leading to the cancellation of the World Series. No such cap was added, and owners hadn’t proposed one again until this summer.
Since the 1991 Twins, the only World Series winners with bottom-half payrolls have been the 2002 Anaheim Angels, 2003 Florida Marlins and 2017 Houston Astros.
“It’s how the game is played in the moment dictates winning outcomes,” agent Scott Boras said Friday. “There’s no question that the probabilities of winning, success, are increased with greater talent, but we all know that talent has many variables as to how it performs at times.”
MLB owners have proposed a salary cap with a floor, a system players say they will never accept. A lockout is likely to start Dec. 2.
Opening-day payrolls were topped by the Mets ($358.4 million), Dodgers ($323.3 million) and Yankees ($302.8 million). The Brewers were at $125.9 million, the Rays $90.5 million and the Guardians $75.5 million.
“Don’t believe what you hear from the owner who’s complaining: ‘I don’t have the resources to compete,’” players association head Bruce Meyer said at the All-Star Game. “They all have the resources to compete. Our proposals include provisions that would give them more resources and reward the teams that actually do compete.”
Manfred maintains spending big increases the odds of success.
“It defies human experience to ask a fan to think that the bottom end of that gap has the same opportunity to win as the top,” he said. “There is no question that everybody in any sport is not going to win once every 30 or 32 years depending on how many teams you have, but the data in our sport is stark: Your opportunity to make the playoffs if you are a larger-market team is dramatically higher and your opportunity to proceed to the subsequent rounds, that advantage grows with each round.”

item.title: [Jays Journal] 3 players the Blue Jays could target if they entertained a Brandon Valenzuela trade
item.dc:creator: Matthew Sookram
item.description: Brandon Valenzuela began the 2026 season as catching depth, but when the season was over he had seemingly solidified himself as the backup catcher for the foreseeable future for the Toronto Blue Jays.
