item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Why Phillies Trying to Trade Trea Turner Feels Impossible
item.dc:creator: Nick Ziegler; Unknown
item.description: As the Philadelphia Phillies prepare for the offseason, the team is going to have a lot of different areas to address. Coming off a disappointing year by their standards, what the Phillies do this offseason is going to be interesting to watch. Philadelphia is a team that has pulled off the impressive feat of being able to reach the postseason for five straight years. item.content:encoded:
As the Philadelphia Phillies prepare for the offseason, the team is going to have a lot of different areas to address.
Coming off a disappointing year by their standards, what the Phillies do this offseason is going to be interesting to watch. Philadelphia is a team that has pulled off the impressive feat of being able to reach the postseason for five straight years.
While many teams would be pleased with that feat, the Phillies are a franchise that has World Series or bust expectations. Philadelphia has a high payroll and a lot of star power. Unfortunately, it really hasn’t panned out of late.
Now, with another year of being eliminated early in October, there is a possibility that the team will look to shake things up. There have already been some rumblings that big names could be available for the Phillies, and not surprisingly, Trea Turner’s name has been mentioned.
However, coming off a bad season with a massive contract, trading him seems like it could be an impossible task for Philadelphia.
Trying to Trade Turner Seems Impossible
One of the reasons why the lineup didn’t live up to their expectations this season was because of the performance of Turner. The former All-Star shortstop had the worst year of his career, slashing .242/.297/.378 with 18 home runs, 58 RBI, and 21 stolen bases; it was the lowest OPS that he had in a proper season.
At 33 years old, the down season at the plate should be seen as a major concern for the team. Furthermore, while the offensive numbers weren’t good, neither was his play defensively.
There has to be some conversation this offseason about him switching positions. Shortstop is too important on the field not to have a good defender there, and Turner struggled a lot.
While the Phillies might look to shop him this winter, it is hard to imagine that it would gain any traction. At 33 years old, struggling defensively, having the worst year of his career at the plate, and the massive contact he has makes it seem like he would be one of the hardest players in the league to trade.
The 33-year-old still has seven years at just over $27 million left on his contract. Unless the Phillies were to eat a significant amount of this deal, it’s hard to imagine that any team would be interested. While it’s not impossible, it's safe to say that it’s highly improbable that Philadelphia will be able to move him.
Nick Ziegler is an alumnus of the Connecticut School of Broadcasting. He has been working in sports media covering the NFL, NBA, MLB, and NHL for nearly a decade with various publications online. With his free time, Nick enjoys being at the Jersey Shore with his wife, daughter, and their golden retriever. You can follow him on X, formerly Twitter, @NickZiegler20.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] What Would an Adley Rutschman Extension Look Like?
item.dc:creator: Zach Coe

item.content:encoded:
RedSoxRoundtable's Zach Coe discusses the calculus the Red Sox have to make when considering a potential contract extension for All-Star catcher Adley Rutschman. Be sure to join out FREE community over on RedSoxRoundtable.com!
The Boston Red Sox made a massive gamble ahead of the trade deadline, sending a massive haul of prospects to the Baltimore Orioles in exchange for three-time All-Star catcher Adley Rutschman. After underperforming in 32 games with Boston, Rutschman now enters his final year of salary arbitration. But the Red Sox face a tough decision on whether to try to extend Rutschman ahead of the 2027 season.
Here's what a potential extension could look like:
What is Rutschman looking for?
Prior to being traded to Boston, Rutschman had exploratory talks with Baltimore about a potential extension. "Rutschman, then, would probably want a deal that makes him a lifetime Oriole, or close to it," wrote The Athletic's Ken Rosenthal on July 6. "His benchmark might be the nine-year, $167 million extension Buster Posey signed with the San Francisco Giants in March 2013," he continued.
The idea that Rutschman could be in line for a deal like Posey's, who will almost assuredly be in Cooperstown in the near future, is a bit far-fetched. Prior to signing that deal, Posey posted a career slash line of .314/.380/.503/.883 with 46 home runs and 191 RBI, winning the 2010 National League Rookie of the Year award, the 2012 National League Most Valuable Player award, and two World Series titles. A far cry from Rutschman's .252/.339/.414/.753 with 74 home runs and 290 RBI, with a career accolade list of three All-Star appearances.
Catchers typically struggle to capitalize on their value given the high injury risk from the wear and tear of being behind the plate nightly. Rutschman is no stranger to those concerns, having played just 189 games over the last two seasons.
Beyond Rutschman's worse resume than Posey's, the Red Sox have shied away from deals that take players well into their 30s, with the longest deal in recent memory being the eight-year extension given to Roman Anthony, which takes him through his age-29 season.
Comparisons
With Posey's nine-year deal seemingly out the window, we'll have to look at some more recent catcher deals, which… gets complicated, to say the least. Of the five richest deals signed by catchers, only one was signed with one year of service time remaining: Toronto Blue Jays' Alejandro Kirk. So let's start there:
Kirk
Ahead of the 2026 season, Kirk signed a five-year, $58-million deal to remain in Toronto through 2030. Before signing, Kirk was a two-time All-Star with a career line of .268/.345/.398/.743. Like Rutschman, Kirk is a strong defensive catcher when it comes to blocking balls in the dirt and framing. However, he struggles to throw runners out.
Though an average annual value of $11.6 million feels low based on Rosenthal's reporting, we'll have to keep looking.
Sean Murphy
At 29, Murphy signed a six-year, $73-million extension with the Atlanta Braves, buying out his final two years of arbitration. According to Spotrac, Murphy was paid $9 million in 2024, his penultimate arbitration year, and $15 million annually for the remainder of the deal.
At the time of signing, Murphy posted a .240/.336/.441/.778 line with 67 home runs and 215 RBI, earning an All-Star selection and becoming one of the game's best defensive catchers.
Cal Raleigh
The runner-up for the 2025 American League Most Valuable Player award, Raleigh signed a six-year, $105-million deal to remain with the Seattle Mariners through the 2030 season, buying out his final three arbitration years. In the four seasons leading up to his extension, Raleigh posted a line of .218/.296/.444/.740 with 93 home runs and 251 RBI. Defensively. Raleigh is a mixed bag, with improving blocking skills, but is middle of the road in both framing and throwing runners out.
Raleigh's deal is also slightly different than the one Rutschman would be looking to sign. While his deal carries an AAV of $17.5 million, the number is lower because he's receiving a lower salary in what would have been his arbitration years. Beginning in 2028, Raleigh will be paid $24.6 million annually.
Will Smith
Will Smith of the Los Angeles Dodgers has the richest catcher contract (by total value). Smith signed a 10-year, $140-million extension with Los Angeles ahead of the 2024 season, buying out his final two arbitration years. However, in typical Dodgers fashion, Smith will be paid $5 million annually from 2034-2043 in deferred payments, lowering the luxury tax hit to just $12 million annually. The deferred payments, expected to be a hot-button topic in ongoing labor talks, paired with Smith being paid through his age-38 season, make the comparison a bit far-fetched.
Before signing the deal, Smith hit .261/.357/.483/.840 with 91 home runs and 306 RBI over five seasons, while providing slightly above-average defense behind the plate.
So... Where does Rutschman fall?
Projecting contracts is an imperfect science. From a strictly production standpoint, Rutschman is most similar to Murphy or Kirk. However, neither player dealt with the same injury problems as Rutschman in the seasons leading up to their extensions. Murphy also represents the closest fit defensively to Rutschman, profiling as one of the best defensive catchers in the sport. The $15 million AAV Murphy would earn from 2025 through 2028 would seem to be the floor of what Rutschman would look for in a potential deal. With MLB Trade Rumors projecting Rutschman to make $9 million in arbitration in 2027, could the Red Sox bump that number up slightly to lower the value of the remainder of the deal to, say, $11 million in 2027 and $14-15 million each year after?
Then, of course, comes the term: catchers especially struggle to cash in on the open market later in their careers. Philadelphia Phillies backstop JT Realmuto posted a line of .257/.315/.384/.700 in 134 games in 2025 before hitting the open market ahead of his age-35 season. Realmuto sat on the free-agent market until Jan. 20, when he signed a three-year, $45-million extension to return to Philadelphia, a move widely criticized as an overpay for a catcher his age.
Red Sox Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow will have to get creative to find common ground with Rutschman. A six-year contract would take him through his age-34 season, having him hit the market at a rather inopportune time. One possible solution for the Red Sox to give Rutschman the long-term commitment he's reportedly seeking could be to front-load the deal, paying him more in his prime while paying him incrementally less as he ages, reducing the franchise's financial burden as he ages and presumably declines.

item.content:encoded:
The Atlanta Braves have endured issues at shortstop all season, and it's no surprise that those challenges have persisted into the MLB playoffs.
Ha-Seong Kim has made a few starts at shortstop, but it could be time for a change, and recently FanSided.com's Chris Landers is urging the Braves manager to make a Ha-Seong Kim change, which feels very obvious at this juncture.
Landers argues that Kim should be tied to the bench for the remainder of the MLB playoffs/NLDS series against the Los Angeles Dodgers:
"This one feels much easier. Of course, Atlanta doesn't have any particularly compelling alternatives at shortstop — it's been one of the themes of this season, really — but at this point, anything is better than another Kim start. The offense has bad enough, but now his defense has become a liability, as he booted a ground ball in the first inning of Game 3."
That would force manager Walt Weiss to go with Mauricio Dubon at short, which would create a ripple effect in the outfield. There are no easy decisions in the MLB playoffs.
More MLB on Heavy: Atlanta Braves Face Major Tyler Mahle Decision After MLB Playoffs
What Should the Braves Do with Ha-Seong Kim?
Atlanta Braves fans, let me know what you would do with Ha-Seong Kim right now??
Kim has seen an influx of playing time since the start of September, but the offensive production still isn't there.
In his last 23 at-bats, Ha-Seong Kim has just one hit, and just a handful of runs scored.
It's been a tough enough season for Kim, which has been well documented, but the October struggles have to be even more frustrating for Braves fans. Kim does not have a hit in the MLB playoffs, and has only reached base a handful of times.
More MLB on Heavy: Ex-New York Mets All-Star Thriving in MLB Playoffs with New Team
Looking at the Atlanta Braves Right Now….
The Atlanta Braves are on the brink of elimination from the MLB playoffs.
Atlanta must win its Game Four contest against the Dodgers on Wednesday evening to stay alive.
It will be interesting to see if manager Walt Weiss makes any changes to the lineup for the elimination game, because it feels like Atlanta could use some sort of shake-up, or change to the regular fold.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Probable Starting Pitchers for Dodgers, Braves, Brewers, Padres in NLDS Game 4
item.dc:creator: Justin Binkowski; Unknown
item.description: Following a heroic relief appearance by San Diego Padres right-hander Michael King, baseball fans will be treated to another day of four Division Series games on Wednesday. The Los Angeles Dodgers beat the Atlanta Braves 3-1 on Tuesday, while the Padres kept their postseason hopes alive with a 4-3 victory over the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 3 of the National League Division Series. item.content:encoded:
Following a heroic relief appearance by San Diego Padres right-hander Michael King, baseball fans will be treated to another day of four Division Series games on Wednesday.
The Los Angeles Dodgers beat the Atlanta Braves 3-1 on Tuesday, while the Padres kept their postseason hopes alive with a 4-3 victory over the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 3 of the National League Division Series. All four teams will be back in action on Wednesday, with San Diego and Atlanta needing a win to stay in the 2026 MLB playoffs.
Here are the expected starting pitching matchups for Game 4 in each NLDS.
Braves vs. Dodgers
Los Angeles right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto delivered another dominant postseason performance on Tuesday, tossing seven innings of one-run ball and striking out 10. With a 2-1 series lead, the Dodgers will now give the ball to another All-Star hurler.
Right-hander Tyler Glasnow will start for Los Angeles in Game 4. The 6-foot-8 righty will make his first playoff appearance of the season on Wednesday after being limited to 13 regular-season starts. But the hard-throwing hurler still had a 3.53 ERA and 98 strikeouts in 74 innings this year. In his career, the 33-year-old has a 4.43 ERA in 16 postseason games (13 starts).
With Atlanta's season on the line, right-hander Tyler Mahle is starting Game 4. The 32-year-old made his MLB postseason debut in the Braves' Wild Card Series matchup with the Philadelphia Phillies, throwing seven innings and allowing just one run. The veteran will try to keep the Dodgers' bats at bay to force a winner-take-all Game 5.
Brewers vs. Padres
With the Padres facing elimination, King pitched the last two innings of Game 3 after starting Game 2. Relievers Mason Miller and Adrian Morejon were unavailable on Tuesday, so Robbie Ray and Joe Musgrove were warming up in the bullpen during the ninth inning of Game 3. With that in mind, San Diego will likely have all hands on deck in Game 4.
The Padres will start right-hander Walker Buehler on Wednesday. The 32-year-old has plenty of postseason experience, posting a 3.04 ERA in 19 career playoff games. But it'll be interesting to see how long of a leash the veteran has in a must-win game for San Diego.
Meanwhile, left-hander Robert Gasser is expected to start Game 4 for the Brewers. The 27-year-old will make his first postseason start after pitching in two games out of the bullpen in the 2025 playoffs. Most notably, though, Gasser starting on Wednesday sets the stage for Jacob Misiorowski to either pitch in the late innings of Game 4 or start Game 5 for Milwaukee if necessary.
Justin Binkowski is a lifelong baseball fan returning to cover the sport he loves after spending nearly a decade writing about video games. Before his time as managing editor at Dot Esports, Binkowski attended King's College in Wilkes-Barre, PA, where he was also a relief pitcher on the school's baseball team. While in college, Binkowski was a media relations intern for the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders during the 2014 season.

item.title: [Blog Red Machine] Reds could find the perfect platoon bat hiding on the White Sox playoff roster
item.dc:creator: Drew Koch
item.description: The Chicago White Sox are looking to punch their ticket to the American League Championship Series, and outfielder Randal Grichuk has been no small part of the team's success in 2026. The White Sox signed Grichuk to a minor-league contract midway through the season after he was designated for assignment by the New York Yankees on April 29. item.content:encoded:
The Chicago White Sox are looking to punch their ticket to the American League Championship Series, and outfielder Randal Grichuk has been no small part of the team's success in 2026.
The White Sox signed Grichuk to a minor-league contract midway through the season after he was designated for assignment by the New York Yankees on April 29. He managed to hit just .194 with a .535 OPS in 16 games with the Bronx Bombers, and elected free agency after clearing waivers on May 1.
He's since played in 101 game for Chicago while posting a .299/.328/.598 slash line. He has 15 home runs and 44 RBI with the White Sox on the season, and has absolutely crushed left-handed pitching throughout his career. This season has been no different, as Grichuk is torturing southpaws to the tune of .327/.371/.655.
Grichuk will be a free agent after the season, and if the Cincinnati Reds have any sense, they'll put a priority on acquiring a right-handed hitting outfielder like Grichuk. If it feels like we've had this conversation every offseason for the last three years, it's because we have.
Reds need to sign a platoon bat like White Sox outfielder Randal Grichuk
Grichuk signed a one-year, $2 million deal with the Arizona Diamondbacks in 2024 and posted an .875 OPS. The Reds added right-handed bats like Bubba Thompson, Stuart Fairchild, and Santiago Espinal during that same offseason.
Grichuk's success led him to signing a one-year, $5 million deal to stay in Arizona that winter. Cincinnati went with Austin Hays, Connor Joe, and Espinal (again). Admittedly, Grichuk struggled during his second year with the D-backs and was traded to the Kansas City Royals at the deadline.
And, as mentioned previously, the veteran outfielder joined the Yankees on a minor-league deal last February before finding his way to the South Side of Chicago.
The point is, the Reds almost always need a right-handed hitting outfielder to platoon with the plethora of left-handed bats to set up shop on the outfield grass. Of the six outfielders on the Reds' 40-man roster, three are left-handed bats (JJ Bleday, Carlos Jorge, and Héctor Rodríguez), and the presumed starters heading into next season.
One of the Reds' right-handed options — Blake Dunn — could miss the entire 2027 season after undergoing elbow surgery this past year. Noelvi Marte, another right-handed bat, could be non-tendered next month, and at best, will start the season in the minor leagues. That leaves Dane Myers as the lone right-handed option in the Reds' outfield.
Reds' president of baseball operations Nick Krall recently spoke about the need to find "complimentary players", and Grichuk certainly fits that mold. Though he's had success this season, at 35 years old, Grichuk won't command a huge contract on the open market.
Giving manager Terry Francona players he can mix and match based on certain situations needs to be one of Krall's biggest priorities this winter. If there's always a need to find someone with Grichuk's makeup, why not just sign the real deal this offseason?

item.content:encoded:
One thing that Boston Red Sox chief baseball officer Craig Breslow has shown multiple times since taking over the organization is that he's not afraid to make a splash in the trade market.
If you look at the Red Sox's 2026 roster, you'll notice a handful of guys were added by way of trade. Garrett Crochet, Sonny Gray, Erik Miller, Johan Oviedo, Adley Rutschman, Curtis Mead, Andruw Monasterio, Caleb Durbin, Eli White and Willson Contreras, among others. The trade market has been Boston's avenue of choice to improve and nothing should be ruled out this winter. Sure, Boston's farm system isn't as good as it was a few years ago, in large part due to the trades, as well as promotions to the big leagues. But there are still plenty of pieces that could be used to bring talent to town this winter.
Arguably, the perfect fit would be Bryce Harper of the Philadelphia Phillies. The Athletic's Ken Rosenthal and USA Today's Bob Nightengale both have insinuated that Harper could be floated by the Phillies this offseason as a potential trade chip, if he is willing to waive his no-trade clause. We already have made the case for why he would be a great fit for Boston. But what could an actual trade look like? Here's a mock trade both sides should consider.
Red Sox Receive: OF/1B Bryce Harper
Phillies Receive: OF Jarren Duran, INF/OF Kristian Campbell, SP Tanner Houck
It's important to note that this is a mock trade. It's far more difficult to actually get a deal done, rather than talking about the idea. When it comes to Harper, the most important variables are whether the Phillies actually would be interested in trading the two-time MVP and then whether he would even be willing to waive his no-trade clause. If the answer to both of those questions was, "yes." Then, you could proceed.
The Phillies notably had a shaky outfield in 2026, plus Adolis Garcia is heading to free agency. Duran had a tough 2026 season, but this is also a guy who had 9.0 wins above replacement in 2024 and 4.9 wins above replacement in 2025. There are reasons to believe that he could get back to that level. Campbell would be the jewel of the deal. He's just 24 years old and already has a long-term deal. He could play in the outfield, or replace Luis Arraez in the infield.
When it comes to Houck, he's someone who is healthy now and who was an All-Star in his last full season in 2024. He got hurt in 2025 and missed all of the 2026 season, except the regular season finale. Still, he could either help in the rotation, or in the bullpen. Houck was selected in the first round of the MLB Draft in 2017, when Dave Dombrowski was still Boston's president of baseball operations.
Again, the idea of a Harper deal is a pipe dream right now. If the Phillies shop him and he is willing to waive his no-trade clause, then this could be more realistic. But there are also finances involved. He has five years left on his deal and will make just over $27 million in 2027 and 2028. Then, he'll make just over $23 million in each of the final three seasons. Are the Red Sox willing to take on that type of money? It would be better than spending something similar on Randy Arozarena or Seiya Suzuki.

item.title: [MLB.com] Turang, Yelich key to Crew wrapping up NLDS
item.dc:creator: Mark Sheldon
item.description: SAN DIEGO -- It sure felt like forever since Christian Yelich notched a postseason RBI. And it was way too long before Brice Turang got his first hit against the Padres in this National League Division Series. Still, the Brewers will need to get more from both players to help them advance to the next round, and perhaps beyond, after being handed a 4-3 loss in Tuesday's Game 3 as the Padres stayed alive for another day and now trail, 2-1, in the best-of-five series. item.content:encoded:
SAN DIEGO -- It sure felt like forever since Christian Yelich notched a postseason RBI. And it was way too long before Brice Turang got his first hit against the Padres in this National League Division Series.
Still, the Brewers will need to get more from both players to help them advance to the next round, and perhaps beyond, after being handed a 4-3 loss in Tuesday's Game 3 as the Padres stayed alive for another day and now trail, 2-1, in the best-of-five series.
One of several missed opportunities for Milwaukee came in the fifth inning. The Brewers had already scored a tying run and then had the bases loaded and two outs when Turang grounded softly to shortstop Xander Bogaerts for a fielder's choice to keep from adding on.
"Trying to get a good pitch to hit. Just didn’t work out," Turang said. "It’s all right. We’ve got to move on and go win tomorrow."
That out made Turang 0-for-10 in the series and 2-for-40 (.050) with 14 strikeouts over his last 11 postseason games. The hitless skid ended when he lofted a two-out single to left field just out of reach for a diving Jase Bowen in the seventh inning.
"I’ve hit some balls right to people and had some good at-bats. I’ve just got to keep working, keep pushing forward," Turang said. "You just want to get better every day."
Yelich, the recently minted team captain and Milwaukee's longest-tenured star, picked up Turang by scorching a 107.2 mph liner to left-center field for an RBI single. It was his first RBI in a playoff game since his first-inning home run in Game 7 of the 2018 NL Championship Series vs. the Dodgers in a losing effort.
Both hitters got another chance to come through for Milwaukee in the top of the ninth inning. Turang worked a walk against Padres pitcher Michael King to put runners on first and second base with one out.
Yelich followed by blistering a first-pitch slider from King at 107.1 mph, only to see it one-hop directly to Bogaerts at shortstop, who turned the game-ending double play.
"A step to the right or left, it's pretty good," Yelich said. "I hit it hard. Just happened to be right at them. It's unfortunate. Part of the game. It's just how it goes sometimes. You've just got to keep battling. Not much else you can do. It is frustrating when it doesn't really bounce your way, but that's how it goes."
Although he’s driven in just the one run in this series, Yelich is batting .400 (4-for-10) with a double. He got the Brewers' first hit in all three games, and in the Game 2 thriller he drew a one-out walk that led to Jackson Chourio's two-run, walk-off single.
"He's looked great," Brewers hitting coach Eric Theisen said. "He's been on time. He's had some hard contact. As a team, we've had hard contact and some loud outs."
As for Turang, he was the Major League leader for September in average (.361) and on-base percentage (.475) before hitting the schneid in October.
"I think he's working his process, same as he always does, working his ABs," Theisen said. "We've seen some good swings. We've seen him put together some good ABs. The results haven't come. But he's continuing to work day to day the same way he always does. I still think he's in a good spot. Keep plugging away."
Sometimes a hit -- even a soft one -- can break the spell, but Theisen didn't put too much stock in Turang's bloop single.
"It's great that the ball falls and you get a knock and get on base. But the pitch-to-pitch approach and the way he's navigating at-bats is what's important," Theisen said. "The process is what's important."
Milwaukee left 11 men on base and missed multiple opportunities to take control of the game that would have given them an NLDS sweep. Besides Turang and Yelich, Chourio went 0-for-4 with a fifth-inning sacrifice fly. He was robbed of a hit by center fielder Jackson Merrill's great catch on the warning track to open the game. Bauers went 0-for-4 with four strikeouts and a walk.
"We had some really good at-bats, hit the ball hard, put ourselves in a good position to win the game. Sometimes you just need that big hit. We’ve got to focus on winning tomorrow," Turang said. "The quality of at-bats that we’ve had has been really cool to see. We’ll get it going. I trust everybody in this locker room."
Said Theisen: "Not everybody's been hot all year long, and it seems like the lineup is deep. When one or two guys have a stretch of games or two or three where maybe they're not producing like they always do, somebody steps up and does it. That's the beautiful thing about this offense and what we've shown all year."
Now the Brewers need to show it in Game 4.

item.content:encoded:
The 2026 MLB playoffs have arrived!
The 12-team postseason began with an action-packed wild-card round that featured eight teams battling for four spots to advance to the eight-team division series.
The Chicago White Sox became the first team to win a series this postseason with a wild-card round sweep of the Houston Astros. Then the New York Yankees swept the Boston Red Sox in two routs, recording the highest series run differential in the history of the current wild-card format. The San Diego Padresalso sealed their spot in the NLDS with a sweep of the Chicago Cubs. In the only wild-card series to go the distance, the Atlanta Braves held off the Philadelphia Philliesto move on.
From the first pitch of the wild-card games to the last out of the World Series, we've got you covered with the postseason bracket, schedules, results and how to watch every game this October.

item.content:encoded:
Both American League Division Series could end as early as Wednesday.
The Tampa Bay Rays and Chicago White Sox each have a 2-0 lead in their ALDS matchups against the New York Yankees and the Cleveland Guardians, respectively. With New York and Cleveland's seasons on the line, both teams may not hesitate to call on their bullpens early and often.
Here are the expected starting pitchers for Game 3 in both ALDS showdowns.
Guardians vs. White Sox
The White Sox have relied on their bullpen throughout the postseason so far, and that trend seems set to continue in Game 3. Chicago is scheduled to start left-hander Sean Newcomb on Wednesday. The 33-year-old had a 3.09 ERA in 60 games for the White Sox this year, and he most recently threw two innings of relief in Game 2 against Cleveland.
Chicago could turn to several different options after Newcomb's presumptive short outing as an opener, including Davis Martin, Erick Fedde, David Sandlin, and Noah Schultz. Left-hander Hagen Smith could also play a role for the White Sox in the later innings, even though he started Game 1 in both the Wild Card Series and the ALDS.
Just like Chicago, Cleveland plans to use an opener on Wednesday. Right-hander Daniel Espino is expected to start for the Guardians in Game 3. The 25-year-old made his MLB debut earlier this year, producing a 4.11 ERA in 14 regular-season games with Cleveland. But the hard-throwing righty also didn't pitch more than two innings in a big-league outing this season. While Tanner Bibee, Foster Griffin, and Joey Cantillo should be among the options to follow Espino in a bulk role, the Guardians will likely have everyone available as they face elimination.
Rays vs. Yankees
Unlike the other American League Division Series, Game 3 between the Rays and Yankees will feature a more straightforward pitching matchup. New York will start left-hander Max Fried, while Tampa will counter with right-hander Nick Martinez on Wednesday.
Fried threw six innings of one-run ball against the Boston Red Sox in the Wild Card round. Martinez, on the other hand, will make his first career postseason start on Wednesday. The 36-year-old has a 3.18 ERA in eight career relief appearances in the playoffs. The Tampa Bay hurler will try to keep New York's bats quiet after the Yankees scored just two runs in the first two games of the ALDS on two Ben Rice homers.
Justin Binkowski is a lifelong baseball fan returning to cover the sport he loves after spending nearly a decade writing about video games. Before his time as managing editor at Dot Esports, Binkowski attended King's College in Wilkes-Barre, PA, where he was also a relief pitcher on the school's baseball team. While in college, Binkowski was a media relations intern for the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders during the 2014 season.

item.content:encoded:
How Braves' Ronald Acuna Jr. has impressed analyst despite quiet playoffs showing appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Atlanta Braves won the 2021 World Series without Ronald Acuna Jr., but they are unlikely to go all the way in 2026 unless the franchise pillar comes alive in the playoffs. He was hitting just .167 with a .485 OPS through his last 18 at-bats entering Tuesday's National League Division Series battle versus the Los Angeles Dodgers. One broadcaster is not worried, however.
"He's been okay in the postseason — he hasn't been the superstar yet — but we feel like his moment is coming. Sooner than later," Braves color analyst C.J. Nitkowski told the "Foul Territory" podcast. "The thing I have been impressed with is he's not necessarily become a guy who's pressing. There are times you're watching at-bats and you know he wants to do something big, and you're thinking 'man, he's going to chase here.' And he doesn't.
"He's been under control. It hasn't happened for him just yet… but nobody's worried about the health of Ronald Acuna Jr. {or} his ability to put up big moments here in the postseason."
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
Ronald Acuña Jr. has wisely avoided pressing in big moments, and it's caught @CJNitkowski's eye…
"He hasn't been the superstar yet, but we feel like his moment is coming sooner rather than later." pic.twitter.com/AJSdOfJVi1
— Foul Territory (@FoulTerritoryTV) October 6, 2026
Players live and die by their approach in this sport, and if their process proves successful, the hits will come. The prodigiously talented Acuna believes he will deliver for the Braves when they need him most. Former MVP Award winners tend to be confident, and for good reason. He eventually erupted in the regular season, and fans are trusting him to do the same in October.
Acuna has endured his struggles during this time of the year, however. He owns a .769 OPS through 34 playoff games, which is nearly 130 points lower than his career output. That still might be enough to help Atlanta move forward.
The 28-year-old right fielder is eying his first extra-base hit of the 2026 postseason during a pivotal Game 3 NLDS clash. Ronald Acuna Jr. is still finding ways to contribute, scoring a run in his four previous games, but one big knock could open the flood gates in Truist Park.

Ronald Acuña Jr. is dealing with right knee soreness.

Acuña appeared to suffer the injury when he slid feet-first into second on a stolen base attempt during Game 2 in Los Angeles. The 28-year-old franchise cornerstone remains in Atlanta’s lineup at DH to face Dodgers ace Yoshinobu Yamamoto in Game 3 at Truist Park on Wednesday evening. It’ll be Lane Thomas heading out to take his spot in right field. It doesn’t appear to be a significant concern, but the Braves clearly aren’t going to take any chances by exposing him to additional wear and tear from a defensive standpoint that would jeopardize his availability moving forward in the postseason.

item.title: [MLB.com] Rays-Yankees ALDS Game 3 FAQ (Wed., 8 p.m. ET, TBS/HBO Max)
item.dc:creator: Adam Berry; Bryan Hoch
item.description: NEW YORK -- Two weeks ago, the Rays went wild in the visitors’ clubhouse at Yankee Stadium after clinching their first American League East championship in five years. That party started shortly after a win over the Yankees and carried late into the New York night. Could they have another celebration in store in the Bronx? It’s time for the American League Division Series to shift venues, going from the Rays’ home dome at Tropicana Field to Yankee Stadium for Game 3 on Wednesday night. But the R
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK -- Two weeks ago, the Rays went wild in the visitors’ clubhouse at Yankee Stadium after clinching their first American League East championship in five years. That party started shortly after a win over the Yankees and carried late into the New York night.
Could they have another celebration in store in the Bronx?
It’s time for the American League Division Series to shift venues, going from the Rays’ home dome at Tropicana Field to Yankee Stadium for Game 3 on Wednesday night. But the Rays are still right where they want to be, holding a commanding 2-0 lead in the series with three chances to advance to the AL Championship Series.
“It's amazing, man. It's exactly the way we wanted to start the series,” Rays closer Bryan Baker said. “To be able to play in front of these fans in this building and take a 2-0 series lead was exactly what we wanted, so it feels really good right now.”
Maybe home-field advantage is what the Yankees need after coming up empty against Rays ace Drew Rasmussen in Game 1 and kicking the ball around the infield in a mistake-filled Game 2 defeat. Or maybe it’ll help to send left-hander Max Fried to the mound, knowing how tough he’s been on Tampa Bay throughout his career.
“We've got to get over it,” Yankees manager Aaron Boone said after Game 2. “We've responded all year to difficult times, and we've got to do that again. We've got to get ourselves up off the mat.”
Tampa Bay’s pitching staff held what looked like a red-hot New York lineup to only two runs in the first 18 innings of this series. If the Rays keep that up, they could enjoy another champagne-soaked night in the city that never sleeps.
“I think it's sweet either way. Doesn't matter the clubhouse,” Rays center fielder Jonny DeLuca said. “Obviously, going over there, having the chance to do that would be pretty special.”
When is the game and how can I watch it?
First pitch for Game 3 of the Yankees-Rays Division Series is set for 8 p.m. ET on Wednesday at Yankee Stadium. The game will be broadcast on TBS, truTV and HBO Max.
The ALDS will be available in Spanish on UniMas, while Univision’s TUDN Radio will provide Spanish-language audio coverage. ESPN Radio will provide live national coverage of all 2026 MLB Postseason games.
Who are the starting pitchers?
Rays: Nick Martinez, RHP
Key stats: 7-3, 2.38 ERA in 16 road starts this season
After rolling out Rasmussen in Game 1 and Freddy Peralta in Game 2, Martinez was the logical choice for the Rays with the series moving to the Bronx. The veteran right-hander was a reliable presence on the mound for Tampa Bay all season, as he posted a 3.10 ERA over 180 innings while the club went 22-9 in his starts. He was at his best on the road, including two outings in the Bronx. The first-time All-Star held the Yankees to only three runs over 12 innings in their home ballpark.
Yankees: Max Fried, LHP
Key stats: 5-1, 1.81 ERA in 7 career GS vs. Tampa Bay
Fried is coming off a sharp outing against the Red Sox in the decisive Game 2 of the AL Wild Card Series, holding Boston to a run on three hits over six innings. Fried walked one and struck out six, his third postseason start since joining the Yankees.
This will be Fried’s third time facing the Rays this season. He last saw them on Sept. 22 in New York, taking the loss in a 6 2/3-inning effort as Tampa Bay clinched the AL East.
Fried also went up against the Rays on April 11 at Tropicana Field, taking a no-decision after permitting three runs over eight innings. For his career, Fried is 5-1 with a 1.81 ERA in seven starts vs. Tampa Bay, including 3-0 with a 0.84 ERA in three starts during the 2025 season.
What might the starting lineups look like?
Rays: It seems likely the Rays will change things up a bit against the Yankees’ left-handers, opting for the right-handed side of most platoons and leaving their lefty hitters available off the bench. Here’s one potential look for a more right-handed lineup.
Yankees: The Yankees have used the same lefty-heavy lineup three times this postseason against right-handed pitchers, including twice in the ALDS. Boone said he is considering shaking things up for Game 3. Boone said before Game 2 that he was considering starting Anthony Volpe at third base. Jose Caballero and Paul Goldschmidt could also enter the mix.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
Rays: The Rays really couldn’t be in much better shape thanks to their starting rotation. Rasmussen handled eight innings in Game 1, and the duo of Peralta and Ian Seymour combined to work 7 2/3 innings in Game 2. So, their traditional relievers have recorded seven of the 54 outs so far this series: six from Baker and a big one from lefty Cam Booser. They may not turn to Peralta or Seymour in Game 3, but they still have starter Griffin Jax available -- and the Yankees have yet to face setup men Tyler Wells and Kevin Kelly in this series.
Yankees: Ryan Weathers replaced infielder/outfielder Amed Rosario for this series, returning from a left flexor strain sustained in late August. David Bednar, Paul Blackburn and Brent Headrick should all be leaned upon for high-leverage outs. Will Warren is now in the bullpen after appearing in 32 games (29 starts) during the regular season. Warren made one appearance in the Wild Card Series, tossing 1 2/3 innings.
Any injuries of note?
Rays: Nothing new. Everyone who was expected to be available for this series is on the roster. The most notable injury situation to watch moving forward is that of left-hander Shane McClanahan, whose status is unclear except that he will not pitch in this series.
Yankees: Aaron Judge was left off the ALDS roster, though Boone said it was a “close” call. Judge has yet to run the bases as he recovers from a right calf strain, though he has been performing outfield running. He has also been taking numerous live at-bats while throwing. Clarke Schmidt has been ruled out for the remainder of the postseason.
Who is hot and who is not?
Rays: Aranda doesn’t get as much love as the other members of the “Big Three,” but his left-handed bat is key. He hit better than either Caminero or Díaz in September, and he had the lone big hit of the night in Game 1 before picking up two more hits in Game 2. Richie Palacios finished strong, too, posting a .981 OPS with five homers in September before delivering the biggest hit of Game 2, and the Brooklyn native likes hitting against his hometown Yankees. Tampa Bay’s entire rotation surged into the postseason, highlighted by Rasmussen and Peralta, the September AL Pitcher of the Month.
The Rays’ outfield is off to a slow start in this series, offensively, but they all showed the impact they can have by putting the ball in play in Game 2. And their defense has been consistently excellent.
Yankees: Rice has been the Yankees' most productive hitter in the postseason, and given how the ALDS has gone, it hasn't been particularly close. Rice is 7-for-15 (.467) in the playoffs, including his two-homer performance in ALDS Game 2. Rice has four homers and eight RBIs overall. Wells is 5-for-12 (.417) in the playoffs, including a couple of doubles in the ALDS. Everyone except for Rice and Wells has combined to go 1-for-46 (.022) in the ALDS so far.
Anything else fans might want to know?
• The Yankees won four of the six games these clubs played in the Bronx during the regular season, splitting a pair of games in late May, then taking three of four the final week of the season. However, the Rays have already celebrated once at Yankee Stadium, as they clinched the AL East title with a 6-1 win in the second half of a doubleheader on Sept. 22.

The National League’s top-seeded Milwaukee Brewers head to San Diego, California, with a 2-0 lead in their NLDS matchup against the Padres for Game 3 Tuesday night at Petco Park. The Brewers have a chance to advance to the NLCS for the second consecutive year with a win, while the Padres will be fighting to keep their season alive with the help of their home crowd.
The Brewers earned a first-round bye as the No. 1 seed in the NL and home-field advantage throughout the MLB playoffs after finishing the regular season with the best record in the league. While that extra time off during the Wild Card Series has hurt teams with a first-round bye plenty of times in the past, it hasn’t slowed down Milwaukee, which won the first two games of the NLDS against San Diego.
Both games have been one-run contests so far, with Brewers catcher William Contreras playing the hero in Game 1 with his go-ahead solo home run in the seventh inning as Milwaukee went on to win 3-2. The Brewers followed that with a dramatic 4-3 victory in Game 2 when 22-year-old outfielder Jackson Chourio delivered a walk-off two-RBI single against Padres superstar closer Mason Miller.
The Brewers are giving the start to right-hander Dustin May for Game 3. May went 7-9 with a 4.70 ERA across 31 regular season starts between Milwaukee and St. Louis. Tuesday night will be May’s first playoff appearance since he appeared in seven games with the Los Angeles Dodgers in 2020.
The Padres will counter with right-hander Nick Pivetta, who missed a large portion of the season due to injury before making his return on Sept. 7. He posted a 2-0 record with a 1.45 ERA across four starts in September and has pitched really well for San Diego since signing with the team ahead of the 2025 season, owning a 16-7 record with a 2.87 ERA and 0.99 WHIP over the last two regular seasons. Pivetta already made a start for the Padres in the NL Wild Card Series, allowing one run over 3.1 innings against the Chicago Cubs on Sept. 30.

item.title: [BoSox Injection] MLB silently confirms Yankees fans whining about Sonny Gray cheating were wasting their time
item.dc:creator: Katie Manganelli
item.description: Sonny Gray pitched a great game against the New York Yankees in Wild Card Game 2. Chad Tracy pulled him in the fifth inning despite the single run he'd allowed at that point and the Boston Red Sox crumbled from there. During the game, some fans noticed some brown flecks on the right side of Gray's neck, on the same side as his pitching arm. Speculation about cheating ran rampant on social media despite the veteran passing all his in-game hand and glove checks from the umpires. Chris Cotillo on O
item.content:encoded:
Sonny Gray pitched a great game against the New York Yankees in Wild Card Game 2. Chad Tracy pulled him in the fifth inning despite the single run he'd allowed at that point and the Boston Red Sox crumbled from there.
During the game, some fans noticed some brown flecks on the right side of Gray's neck, on the same side as his pitching arm. Speculation about cheating ran rampant on social media despite the veteran passing all his in-game hand and glove checks from the umpires.
Chris Cotillo on October 6 reported that MLB investigated Gray for the potential use of illegal substances. Since Gray has not been officially disciplined by the league and he passed all the in-game examinations, Cotillo assumes he's in the clear.
While it was evident that Gray had something on his neck, it didn't look like pine tar, which can be seen in dark, glossy layers on players' helmets and bats. in April 2024, Yankees pitcher Michael Pineda was ejected for using pine tar, which he rubbed on his neck before the game, to improve his grip on the ball. The pine tar was in a uniform smear on his neck and not pilled up, as whatever was on Gray's neck appeared.
MLB investigated Red Sox's Sonny Gray for rumors of illegal sticky substance use in Wild Card Game 2 against Yankees
If there was something sticky on Gray's neck that remained there after he rubbed his fingers over it before nearly every batter, it would remain on his hands when he presented them to umpires to be checked after every inning.
It wasn't even unique for Gray to touch his neck before every pitch — he's been seen doing the same swiping motion on the side of his neck countless times. Using sweat to increase the stickiness of rosin on one's hands, a completely legal substance, is a trick used by pitchers throughout the league over many years.
Gray was the Sox's ace all season and he gave his teammates a great start in the postseason without cheating. His 2.72 ERA over 169 innings this season and 1.98 ERA in two starts against the Yankees aren't indicative of someone who needs extra, illegal help to get through games.
Gray is an impending free agent and the Sox's 2027 rotation will miss him dearly. He was the only righty in the rotation and his 18 wins matched Garrett Crochet's total in 2025. Both pitchers were incredibly effective stoppers in their full seasons with Boston.
Gray's tenure with the Red Sox didn't end on the best note, as he was dissatisfied with Tracy's decision to pull him so early in the game. But if Boston seeks a reunion with Gray, it can do so in good conscience, knowing he didn't use illegal substances in a playoff game.

item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA -- Ronald Acuña Jr.'s sore right knee led the Braves to limit him to designated hitter duties for Atlanta's 3-1 loss in Game 3 of the National League Division Series on Tuesday night at Truist Park.
Acuña was slated to play right field until the Braves announced the lineup change approximately 90 minutes before the first pitch. The Braves veteran outfielder served as the DH 14 times during the regular season. But this marked the first time he has filled the role during this postseason.
Acuña produced a .997 OPS over his final 26 regular season games, but he entered Tuesday having gone just 3-for-18 through his first five playoff games this year. On Tuesday, he went 0-for-3 with a walk and a strikeout.
Lane Thomas was tabbed to replace Acuña in right field for Tuesday’s game. Sean Murphy was moved to the bench after initially being lined up to serve as Atlanta’s DH in Game 3.

item.dc:creator: Alyssa Norwin

The pro baseball pitcher is hoping to win a championship with the Braves after joining the team in 2024. While Sale has had a lengthy baseball career in the public eye, he mostly keeps his personal life to himself. His wife, Brianne Sale (née Aron), has been by his side through the entirety of his professional playing career, bu
item.content:encoded:
Meet Atlanta Braves Pitcher Chris Sale’s Wife: All About Brianne Aron
Chris Sale is taking the field for the Atlanta Braves in the 2026 Major League Baseball postseason. The pro baseball pitcher is hoping to win a championship with the Braves after joining the team in 2024.
While Sale has had a lengthy baseball career in the public eye, he mostly keeps his personal life to himself. His wife, Brianne Sale (née Aron), has been by his side through the entirety of his professional playing career, but they keep their relationship very private.
However, we managed to dig up some dirt on the couple’s love story. Scroll down to learn more.
Who is Chris Sale’s wife?
Since Chris keeps his relationship private, very little is known about his wife. Her Instagram page is private, and her LinkedIn has not been updated in more than a decade.
What her page does reveal, though, is that she attended Florida Gulf Coast University, where she studied public relations and philosophy, and previously worked as a front desk clerk for Embassy Suites from 2008 to 2010. Once Chris was drafted, it’s possible she put career plans on the back burner to support him and raise their family.
How did Chris Sale meet his wife?
Chris and Brianne seemingly met when they were both students at FGCU. Chris left college after his junior year to enter the 2010 MLB Draft, and Brianne was also a student at the university when Chris was playing baseball there.
While it’s unclear exactly when these two got together, they tied the knot in 2011, just as Chris’ professional career was taking off. Brianne seemingly moved to Chicago with Chris while he was playing for the White Sox from 2010 to 2016, as her LinkedIn lists her as living in the “greater Chicago area.”
Does Chris Sale have kids?
Yes, Chris and Brianne are parents to three children. Their eldest son, Rylan, was born in 2010, before Chris and Brianne tied the knot. They later welcomed another son, Brayson, and their third son, Camden.
Chris has been open about how much he struggles with not being there for some of the big moments in his kids’ lives because of his career.
“You can ask my mom, ask my dad, ask my sister, ask anybody in my family … my dad missed less than a handful of my games until I got to college,” he once said. “Going from that to me missing my kids’ first day of school, missing my son’s first Little League game, missing practices, missing games, not being there just for stuff … it’s hard.”

In a game that could have a massive shift in momentum in either direction for both teams, the Atlanta Braves bring future HOFer Chris Sale to the mound amidst one of the best seasons of his career against Yoshinobu Yamamoto during the best season of his young career.
The last time these two pitchers faced off the Braves beat the Dodgers 1-0 when Chris Sale pitched a complete game shutout on August twenty-seventh. A repeat of that exact result is slim, but if Sale could pitch a long game today, it would be welcomed among the bullpen that has already had back-to-back games where they carried the load.
Drake Baldwin was the offensive hero the last time the Braves faced Yamamoto with a solo shot that was the only run of the game.
First pitch is at 6:00 pm EDT. Follow along in the comments.

item.title: [Yanks Go Yard] William Contreras trade could elevate the energy of Yankees-Red Sox rivalry
item.dc:creator: Stephen Parello
item.description: One of the New York Yankees prime trade deadline needs was believed to be the catcher position. It seemed like a foregone conclusion that the club would target help behind the plate, as Austin Wells struggled miserably throughout the first half of the season. Brian Cashman seemed to feel otherwise. Wells rebounded somewhat in the second half, hitting .229/.351/.436 down the stretch. Still, the Yankees might not want to roll into 2026 with Wells, or at least might be wary of counting on him as th
item.content:encoded:
One of the New York Yankees prime trade deadline needs was believed to be the catcher position. It seemed like a foregone conclusion that the club would target help behind the plate, as Austin Wells struggled miserably throughout the first half of the season. Brian Cashman seemed to feel otherwise.
Wells rebounded somewhat in the second half, hitting .229/.351/.436 down the stretch. Still, the Yankees might not want to roll into 2026 with Wells, or at least might be wary of counting on him as the primary catcher moving forward. There will be options in free agency, highlighted by Ryan Jeffers, but after him there's Tyler Stephenson and a bunch of questionable options. The bidding for Jeffers could get hot, so New York might turn to the trade market to scratch its itch behind the dish.
That could bring a risky trade partner back into the fold: the Milwaukee Brewers, who could find themselves dangling William Contreras in order to bring back a haul.
Trading the soon-to-be 29-year-old would follow the Brewers' M.O. He'll be entering his final year of team control in 2027, and his last two seasons have been good, but a downgrade from his peak in 2023 through 2024. This season, Contreras hit .270/.341/.417 with 18 homers, which is good production regardless of position, but looks even better in light of the fact that he's a catcher
| William Contreras fWAR by year since becoming a regular |
|---|
| 2023 - 5.8 |
| 2024 - 5.5 |
| 2025 - 3.7 |
| 2026 - 3.0 |
A Yankees-Brewers William Contreras trade would be a Devin Williams type of risk that further ignites Red Sox rivalry
Whether Devin Williams flopped because he was on the decline or because he just didn't want to play in New York is unclear, but Milwaukee has a history of fleecing people in these kinds of trades. Just look at what they did to the Mets with Freddy Peralta for further proof.
There's a real reason to engage the Brewers with caution, even for an offensive force at catcher like Contreras. However, if Brian Cashman made a move for the backstop, he'd be throwing even more gas on the Yankees' never-ending rivalry with the Boston Red Sox.
The Red Sox employ William's older brother, Willson Contreras, so such a move would add a sibling rivalry dynamic to the competition between these long-standing enemies. Willson is fiery player, who has both taken Boston's leadership to task while also threatening to use his no-trade clause if the Red Sox approached him about a trade prior to Boston's turn of fortune ahead of the deadline.
William is an equally passionate player, following in his older brother's footsteps with stirring displays of emotion on the field. Putting the two of them together, on opposite sides of the most heated rivalry in sports, would create a highly combustible situation that could be a lot of fun to watch.
It's all speculation for now. The Brewers have shown no indication that they'd want to trade Contreras, and we'd have to admit that while he'd be an intriguing option, we'd be wary if they actively shopped him. At the same time, if he landed in pinstripes and it worked out, next year's Yankees-Red Sox matchups could be full of fireworks and a lot of fun.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated Lifestyle] MLB WAG Reagan Bregman Shares Her On-the-Go Wellness Tips for Busy Moms
item.dc:creator: Cara O’Bleness; Unknown
item.description: When it comes to fitness and nutrition, Reagan Bregman has her routine down to a science. The proud mom of two and wife of Chicago Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman is often on the go, so she has created a health and wellness routine that adapts to her busy schedule. “I typically get in three to four workouts a week, though I’m always trying to fit in more,” she tells SI Lifestyle. “We travel so much and life with two kids can be unpredictable, so I’ve learned to just fit it in when I can, even if
item.content:encoded:
When it comes to fitness and nutrition, Reagan Bregman has her routine down to a science. The proud mom of two and wife of Chicago Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman is often on the go, so she has created a health and wellness routine that adapts to her busy schedule.
“I typically get in three to four workouts a week, though I’m always trying to fit in more,” she tells SI Lifestyle. “We travel so much and life with two kids can be unpredictable, so I’ve learned to just fit it in when I can, even if it’s 30 minutes in a hotel or an hour in the gym. My routine is a mix of mostly weightlifting with some classes mixed in, like Pilates and tennis.”
Where nutrition is concerned, Reagan lives by an 80/20 principle that allows her to occasionally indulge while primarily listening to her intuition where food is concerned. She loves a good stir fry bowl, mixing together Japanese barbecue sauce, rice, protein and whatever veggies she has on hand in the fridge at any given moment.
“Nutrition is definitely important to me, but I try not to make it overly complicated,” she says. “ ... Most days, especially at home, I try to eat whole foods and get protein. But I also love going out to dinner, ordering dessert and getting pizza with my kids. I think it’s important to learn about nutrition and know what your body needs so you know what works for you most of the time.”
Since welcoming their eldest son, Knox, in August 2022 and Bennett in April 2025, the Bregmans have moved around quite a bit. While Alex was with the Houston Astros through 2024, he played one season with the Boston Red Sox in 2025 before signing a multi-year contract with the Cubs earlier this year. Outside of baseball, the family loves to give back and is very philanthropy oriented. In addition to serving on the board of Bregman Cares, a nonprofit that focuses on autism advocacy, Reagan also works with The Cities project, which supports Chicago Public Schools and their families.
“I live by the saying that you can’t pour from an empty cup,” Reagan says. “As moms, I think we can feel guilty for taking time for ourselves, but I’ve learned that I’m a better mom when I do. It’s important to put systems in place that give you a break, whether that’s leaning on family, hiring help if you're able to or trading off with your partner. It doesn't have to be a perfect wellness routine either; sometimes it’s a 20-minute workout or just a walk. I think the biggest thing is realizing that taking care of yourself isn’t separate from taking care of your family.”
More SI Lifestyle news
Cara is a trending news writer/editor for Sports Illustrated Swimsuit. A passionate writer and editor with more than 10 years of experience in print and online media, she loves storytelling and believes that words have the power to change the world. Prior to joining the team, Cara worked as a writer and editor across a number of content verticals, including food, lifestyle, health and wellness, and small business and entrepreneurship. In her free time, Cara loves reading, spending time with her family and making her way through Michigan’s many microbreweries. She is a graduate of Michigan State University's School of Journalism.

item.title: [MLB.com] Facing Sale in key Game 3, Dodgers drop Ohtani to 5th in lineup
item.dc:creator: Sonja Chen
item.description: ATLANTA -- Shohei Ohtani dropped to fifth in the order, one of several lineup tweaks with the Dodgers facing left-hander Chris Sale and the Braves in Game 3 of the NL Division Series on Tuesday night at Truist Park with the series tied 1-1. The last time that Ohtani started in the five-hole or lower was Sept. 23, 2020, while he was with the Angels. Ohtani had previously only started in the first or second spot for the Dodgers. When manager Dave Roberts discussed the lineup change with Ohtani, th
item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA -- Shohei Ohtani dropped to fifth in the order, one of several lineup tweaks with the Dodgers facing left-hander Chris Sale and the Braves in Game 3 of the NL Division Series on Tuesday night at Truist Park with the series tied 1-1.
The last time that Ohtani started in the five-hole or lower was Sept. 23, 2020, while he was with the Angels. Ohtani had previously only started in the first or second spot for the Dodgers.
When manager Dave Roberts discussed the lineup change with Ohtani, the superstar made a tongue-in-cheek -- and self-aware -- comment about his performance of late.
"He said, 'I was going to come to you in September and say, why don't you hit me seventh?'" Roberts said. "My point being, he wants to do whatever will help the team. So I feel good about this today. And it's nothing as a sign of what's more to come. It's just for today specifically."
Ohtani entered Tuesday hitting 3-for-15 (.200) with a double, a walk and five strikeouts against Sale.
Other notable changes for the Dodgers included starting Miguel Rojas at second base over Tommy Edman and Kiké Hernández at third over Max Muncy. L.A. stacked its right-handed hitters higher in an effort to counteract Sale.
"Runs are going to be hard to come by," Roberts said. "We all understand that. Sale's going to be tough. But the guys I feel at the top have a good chance to get on base, and I do think that there's going to be opportunities where the game, the situation, bleeds into Shohei's at-bat."
Here is the full lineup:
1. Mookie Betts, SS
2. Freddie Freeman, 1B
3. Teoscar Hernández, LF
4. Will Smith, C
5. Shohei Ohtani, DH
6. Miguel Rojas, 2B
7. Andy Pages, CF
8. Kyle Tucker, RF
9. Kiké Hernández, 3B
Game 3 is a matchup of aces, Sale and Yoshinobu Yamamoto -- and a rematch of the Braves' and Dodgers' final regular-season meeting on Aug. 27. Yamamoto allowed a leadoff homer and nothing else across 6 1/3 innings, but he was outdueled by Sale, who tossed a shutout on 109 pitches.
Tuesday's contest comes with higher stakes, as the loser will be at risk of elimination in Game 4 on Wednesday. So Roberts acted with urgency with his lineup configuration.
Ohtani hit 2-for-8 in the first two games of the NLDS, but he's chasing pitches outside the zone at a 42.9% clip (nine swings on 20 pitches out of the zone), up from 30% in the regular season. The swing decisions may partially be a product of his overall rust, as Ohtani appeared in just eight games in September due to an IL stint to manage lingering right biceps and left knee injuries.
Even if Ohtani is not quite right -- both physically and with his swing -- the Dodgers still expect him to take quality at-bats and not allow the Braves to expand the zone, which he has not done with consistency thus far.
"They're going to expand as much as you're going to let them," Roberts said. "I think, for me, it's just clear that they're trying to stay away until he kind of shows some more restraint. So I think he understands that it's more of once you get in the box and how you're going to be able to control your emotions and check down."
Since returning from the IL, Ohtani has led off vs. right-handers and hit second vs. left-handers. As Roberts said, dropping Ohtani to fifth was more about the approach against Sale than any indication of how future lineups might look.
Roberts said he doesn't see Ohtani hitting fifth in Game 4 vs. Braves right-hander Tyler Mahle, but for Game 3, he felt that moving his superstar down was in the Dodgers' best interest.
"I think it's one of those things that it's not a lack of confidence in any player," Roberts said. "It's more of what I feel gives us the best chance to win today. In a short series, that's the mindset that everyone has to have."

Tatis is hitting for a .289 BA, .358 OBP and .470 SLG with an 18.5% strikeout rate and a 9.1% walk rate. His OPS is .828 and he has scored 96 runs. In 704 plate appearances, he has hit 25 home runs and driven in 83 runs. Tatis has recorded 38 steals on 51 attempts. In his previous game he had a hitless performance (0 for 5) against the Brewers.
Dustin May makes the start for the Brewers, his 32nd of the season. He is 7-9 with a 4.70 ERA and 144 strikeouts in 145 2/3 innings pitched.

item.title: [roundtable.io] How White Sox Turned ‘Organized Chaos’ Into a Postseason Weapon
item.dc:creator: Sam Phalen
item.description: Chicago's unconventional pitching plan has dominated October, but its postseason success was built through a full season of preparation. Now just one win away from advancing to the ALCS, it's becoming undeniable that this group has a little bit of magic to it. These White Sox are young, hungry, and they don't know what they don't know. They show up to the ballpark every day believing they can win. And sometimes in the postseason, that spirit is enough to carry a team. Baseball, however, isn't ju
item.content:encoded:
Chicago's unconventional pitching plan has dominated October, but its postseason success was built through a full season of preparation.
Now just one win away from advancing to the ALCS, it's becoming undeniable that this group has a little bit of magic to it. These White Sox are young, hungry, and they don't know what they don't know.
They show up to the ballpark every day believing they can win. And sometimes in the postseason, that spirit is enough to carry a team.
Baseball, however, isn't just watching Chicago with admiration for the Cinderella story at hand. There's also a somewhat unprecedented strategy being deployed by the White Sox this October, one that could change the way teams shape their pitching staffs moving forward if this level of success continues.
Organized chaos.
That's what the White Sox call their pitching strategy for the postseason.
Right-hander Sean Burke is the only truly reliable traditional starting pitcher the White Sox have on their playoff roster. So Chicago has largely thrown standard pitching roles out the window. Manager Will Venable plays the matchups on a nearly pitch-by-pitch basis, deploying an all-hands-on-deck approach to cover the 27 outs necessary for victory.
Unconventional? Absolutely. But it's also been remarkably effective.
Even Burke hasn't been used as a traditional starting pitcher. And why would he be?
Burke entered Monday's ALDS Game 2 against the Cleveland Guardians in the third inning after Chicago used two openers to begin the game. The White Sox wanted to roll out a pair of left-handers, Anthony Kay and Sean Newcomb, to navigate the top of Cleveland's lineup and neutralize its dangerous left-handed bats before turning things over to Burke.
The strategy also shortened the game for Burke, allowing him to attack hitters without worrying about pacing himself for a traditional six- or seven-inning start.
He was lights out.
Burke pitched into the bottom of the eighth inning and likely could have kept going. At one point, he set a franchise postseason record with 13 consecutive batters retired. Then with the White Sox nursing a 4-2 lead, Venable ultimately decided there was no reason to push it.
The White Sox have now allowed just nine total runs over four postseason games while pitching to a 1.75 team ERA.
All anybody wants to know is how they've managed to make it work. After all, it's not like the White Sox had an incredible pitching staff throughout the regular season. Their 4.12 team ERA was right around the MLB average.
Not to mention, this is an incredibly young White Sox team with plenty of young arms. Many of them are getting their first taste of playoff baseball during this current run. And inexperienced pitchers are usually expected to show some signs of fatigue this late in the season as they blow past previous career highs in innings pitched.
Instead, the opposite has happened. The deeper the White Sox have gotten into the season, the more dominant their pitching staff has become.
So why is it working for Chicago?
Because the White Sox put it into practice during the regular season.
Consistency has been a primary focus for Venable as he takes this young team into the postseason. He wants players in the same positions, doing things they're familiar with. His message in pregame speeches hasn't changed. And when it comes to the pitching staff, they're comfortable being used as Swiss Army knives because that's how they've been deployed all year.
Instead, Chicago learned how to survive without one.
Using an opener in front of a starting pitcher, throwing a bullpen game, asking relievers to cover multiple innings. These are all things the White Sox did during the regular season to get themselves into the playoffs.
Nothing about what Venable is asking his pitchers to do in October is foreign to them. The stakes are higher and the margin for error is smaller, but the roles themselves haven't suddenly changed.
"Organized chaos" from the pitching staff was a necessity for the White Sox to survive 162 games. Now it's becoming a weapon in the postseason.
The young right-hander admitted Chicago's original plan for the game went a bit haywire after Cleveland scored two runs in the first inning, forcing Venable to make an earlier-than-expected move to the bullpen for Newcomb.
But Burke was prepared for the unconventional situation, in part because he leaned on teammates who had already experienced similar roles.
He specifically mentioned Erick Fedde, Sean Newcomb and White Sox bullpen coach Matt Wise as people he leaned on while establishing a routine and rhythm for entering a game after it had already started.
It's another example of why Chicago's organized chaos works. The White Sox aren't improvising in October. They're leaning on the versatility, preparation and experience they spent an entire season developing. Keeping things consistent is an underrated aspect of playoff baseball.
For many teams, the bright lights of October make them tighten up. There's a misconception that you need to play differently and treat these games differently simply because they mean more.
And yes, fundamentally sound baseball becomes increasingly important when the margin for error shrinks. But the White Sox are showing how familiarity, comfort and playing loose can actually be the key to postseason success.
That includes the unconventional approach to team pitching.
It doesn't matter if you're a starter or reliever. It doesn't matter if you're being asked to pitch five innings or throw five pitches. The goal is the same: Get 27 outs.
Guys like Burke are flexible enough to make it work. Venable has continued pushing all the right buttons. And the White Sox have built a pitching staff that's comfortable operating without the traditional roles that have defined the sport for generations.
It started as a necessity during the regular season. It's become one of Chicago's greatest strengths in October.
And if this White Sox playoff run continues, don't be surprised if more teams around Major League Baseball start trying to replicate it.

item.content:encoded:
Brewers' William Contreras ghosted agent for weeks after Braves trade appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
Up 2-0 in their NL Division Series (NLDS) matchup against the San Diego Padres, the Milwaukee Brewers are on the precipice of another NL Championship Series (NLCS) berth. A Game 3 win over the Padres Tuesday night would give the Brewers home-field advantage against the winner of the Los Angeles Dodgers-Atlanta Braves NLDS tilt. On Tuesday, Milwaukee catcher William Contreras appeared on a podcast with former Braves teammate Ronald Acuna Jr. Contreras told his agent to not speak to him for three weeks once the news broke he was heading to Milwaukee, shared by X (formerly Twitter) user Master Flip.
William Contreras stopped talking to his agent for 3 weeks after the Braves traded him to Milwaukee 😳
Acuña: “Did it hurt when you were traded?”
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
Contreras: “Of course, bro. I got over it, but when I got here to Milwaukee in 2024, the vibe wasn’t the same, and I was like, damn.… pic.twitter.com/HAv3ZgXINh
— Master Flip | Phillip Feliz 🇩🇴 (@Masterflip_) October 6, 2026
"December 15th, traded to Milwaukee, and it hit," Contreras stated to his former teammate. "I stopped talking to my agent. I told him, don't text me for 3 weeks; I don't want to talk to you. He tells me no, that it's business, and I said that's not business at all. I kept telling him, send me back to Atlanta. I just thought about the guys there because it was a vibe."
As the NL's top seed, there's a good chance that the Brewers could host the Braves in the NLCS. A win on the road Tuesday night would give the Brew Crew some rest before facing off against either prospective opponent. Last year, the Dodgers dispatched the Brewers in a clean sweep. A match against the Braves would likely favor Milwaukee, who is looking to get back to the World Series for the first time since 1982.
In any case, it looks like Contreras is right at home with the Brewers. He's become a multiple-time All-Star and one of baseball's best all-around catchers. Despite a breakout 2022 campaign, the Braves elected to trade for Athletics All-Star Sean Murphy, sending Contreras up north a few days later. Murphy has declined in Atlanta, mostly due to injuries. 2025 NL Rookie of the Year Drake Baldwin has replaced him. Can Contreras lead the Brew Crew back to the Fall Classic? If so, the trade will have paid off quite well in Milwaukee.
Related: Padres go to extreme lengths to mess with Brewers before do-or-die NLDS Game 3

Be sure to join out FREE community over on RedSoxRoundtable.com!
